Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 59, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surat al-Hashr is Medinan according to the consensus (ijma') of the scholars, and it has twenty-four verses. Ibn 'Abbas narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites Surat al-Hashr, nothing will be left of the Garden, the Fire, the Throne, the Footstool, the heavens, the earth, the insects, the wind, the clouds, the birds, the beasts, the trees, the mountains, the sun, the moon and the angels, but that they will send blessings upon him and seek forgiveness for him. If he dies that same day or night, he dies as a martyr (shahid)." Al-Tha'labi recorded it.

Al-Tha'alibi also recorded, from Yazid al-Raqqashi, from Anas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites the end of Surat al-Hashr, [from] 'Had We sent down this Qur'an upon a mountain' (Al-Hashr: 21) to its end, and dies that night, dies as a martyr." 

Al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ma'qil ibn Yasar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever says three times in the morning, 'I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan,' and recites three verses from the end of Surat al-Hashr, Allah appoints for him seventy thousand angels who will send blessings upon him until evening; and if he dies that day, he dies as a martyr. And whoever recites them in the evening, it is likewise." He said: "This is a hasan (sound) hadith, gharib (strange)."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.﴾ (1)

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 59, verse 2:

2. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering.﴾ There are three issues concerning this.

The first: His saying, ﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas: "Surat al-Hashr?" He said: "Say Surat al-Nadir." They were a group of Jews from the descendants of Harun (peace be upon him). They settled in Madinah during the trials of the Children of Israel, awaiting Muhammad (ﷺ). What befell them is what Allah has stated explicitly.

The second: His saying, ﴿at the first gathering﴾. Al-hashr (gathering) means assembly, and it is of four kinds: two gatherings in this world and two gatherings in the Hereafter. As for the one in this world, it is His saying, ﴿It is He who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering﴾. Al-Zuhri said: They were of a tribe (sibt) [[al-sibt: the son's son. And the sibt among the Jews is like the tribe among the Arabs.]] that had not been struck by exile, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had decreed exile upon them; otherwise He would have punished them in this world [[What is between the two squares is missing from H.]]. The first gathering in this world was their gathering towards Syria. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah said: Whoever doubts that the place of gathering is in Syria, let him recite this verse. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said to them: "Go out." They said: "To where?" He said: "To the land of the gathering." Qatadah said: This is the first gathering. Ibn 'Abbas said: They were the first of the People of the Book to be gathered and expelled from their homeland. It was also said: They were expelled to Khaybar, and the meaning of "at the first gathering" is their expulsion from their fortresses to Khaybar, and its last was 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) expelling them from Khaybar to Najd and Adhri'at. It was also said: Tayma' and Ariha, and that was because of their disbelief and breaking of their covenant. As for the second gathering, it is their gathering near the Final Hour. Qatadah said: A fire will come that gathers people from the east to the west; it will spend the night with them wherever they spend the night, take a midday rest with them wherever they rest, and consume whoever lags behind. This is established in the Sahih, and we have mentioned it in (Kitab al-Tadhkirah). Similarly Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik, who said: I said to Malik, "Is it their exile from their homes?" He said to me: "The gathering on the Day of Resurrection is the gathering of the Jews." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) exiled the Jews to Khaybar when they were asked about the wealth and concealed it, so he deemed their blood lawful on that account. Ibn al-'Arabi said: The gathering has a first, a middle and a last: the first is the exile of Banu al-Nadir, the middle is the exile of Khaybar, and the last is the gathering of the Day of Resurrection. From al-Hasan: They are Banu Qurayzah. But the rest of the commentators disagreed with him and said: Banu Qurayzah were not gathered; rather, they were killed. Related by al-Tha'labi.

The third: Al-Kiya al-Tabari said: Reconciling the people of war on exile from their homes without any compensation is not permissible now; that was only in the early days of Islam and was then abrogated (nusikha). Now there must be fighting against them, or their enslavement, or the imposition of the jizyah upon them.

His saying, ﴿They thought that their fortresses would protect them﴾. He means: because of the great standing of the Jews, their strength and power in the hearts of the Muslims, and the unity of their word.

(And they thought that their fortresses would protect them from Allah.) It was said: They are al-Wati'ah, al-Nata' and al-Salalim and al-Katibah. (From Allah) meaning: from His command. They were people of halqah (weapons) [[i.e., armour/weapons]] in abundance, and of strong fortresses, so nothing from them protected them.

(But Allah came upon them) meaning: His command and His punishment.

(From where they did not expect) meaning: they did not suppose. It was also said: from where they did not know. It was also said: from where they did not expect, by the killing of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, related by Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and Abu Salih.

His saying, ﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾: by the killing of their chief Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. The one who killed him was Muhammad ibn Maslamah, Abu Na'ilah Silkan ibn Salamah ibn Waqsh, who was Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf's foster brother, 'Abbad ibn Bishr ibn Waqsh, al-Harith ibn Aws ibn Mu'adh, and Abu 'Abs ibn Jabr. His report is well known in the biography (sirah). In the Sahih, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been helped with terror over a distance of a month's journey." So how would he not be helped with it over a distance of a mile from Madinah to the quarter of Banu al-Nadir? This is a special privilege of Muhammad (ﷺ) above others.

His saying, ﴿They destroyed their houses with their own hands﴾: the reading of the common people is with light stress, from akhraba, meaning they demolish. Al-Sulami, al-Hasan, Nasr ibn 'Asim, Abu al-'Aliyah, Qatadah and Abu 'Amr read yukhharibuna with the doubled letter, from al-takhrib. Abu 'Amr said: I chose the doubled form because al-ikhrab is leaving a thing in ruin without an occupant, whereas the Banu al-Nadir did not leave it in ruin; rather they wrecked it by demolition, supported by His saying: "by their own hands and the hands of the believers." Others said: al-takhrib and al-ikhrab have the same meaning, and the doubling indicates intensification. Sibawayh related that fa''altu and af'altu are interchangeable, such as akhrabtuhu and kharrabtuhu, and afrahtuhu and farrahtuhu. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the first reading. Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: The believers were demolishing from outside in order to enter, and the Jews were demolishing from inside so that they could rebuild with what had been ruined of their fortress. It is related that they had made a treaty with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that they would be neither against him nor with him. When he prevailed on the day of Badr, they said: "He is the Prophet described in the Torah, so his banner shall not be turned back." When the Muslims were defeated on the day of Uhud, they doubted and broke the covenant. Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf set out with forty riders to Makkah, and they formed an alliance with Quraysh at the Ka'bah. The Prophet (ﷺ) then commanded Muhammad ibn Maslamah al-Ansari, who killed Ka'b by treachery, and then attacked them at dawn with the battalions. He said to them: "Leave Madinah." They said: "Death is dearer to us than that," and they called to war. It was also said: They asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for ten days to prepare for departure, so 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy the hypocrite and his companions sent to them: "Do not leave the fortress; if they fight you, we are with you and will not forsake you; and if you are expelled, we will go out with you." So they fortified the alleys and reinforced them for twenty-one nights. When Allah cast terror into their hearts and they despaired of the support of the hypocrites, they sought reconciliation, but he refused them except exile, as will be explained. Al-Zuhri, Ibn Zayd and 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) made peace with them on the condition that they might take whatever the camels could carry, they used to admire the beam and the pillar, so they would demolish their houses and load that onto their camels, and the believers would destroy what remained. Also from Ibn Zayd: They used to destroy them so that the Muslims would not dwell in them after them. Ibn 'Abbas said: Whenever the Muslims gained control of one of their houses, they would demolish it to widen the space for battle; and they would breach their houses from behind into the next one to fortify themselves within, and throw at the Muslims from those they had been expelled from. It was also said: so that they could block their alleys with them. 'Ikrimah said: "by their own hands" refers to ruining their interiors and what was in them, lest the Muslims take it; and "by the hands of the believers" refers to ruining their exteriors, so that they might reach them through that. 'Ikrimah said: Their dwellings were ornamented, and they envied the Muslims that they should live in them, so they ruined them from inside, and the Muslims ruined them from outside. It was also said: They ruin their houses by breaking the agreement, and "the hands of the believers" by fighting; this was said by al-Zuhri as well. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala said: "by their own hands" refers to their leaving them, and "by the hands of the believers" refers to their expulsion from them. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Demolition for corruption is literal when done by hand, and metaphorical when done by breaking the covenant; yet al-Zuhri's view on the metaphorical is more fitting than that of Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So take warning, O people of insight.﴾ That is: learn a lesson, O people of intellect and understanding. It was also said: O you who witnessed that with your sight, since it is the plural of basar (sight). Among the aspects of this lesson: they took refuge in their fortresses from Allah, so Allah brought them down from them. Among its aspects also: He gave power over them to those who used to support them. And among its aspects too: they demolished their own wealth with their own hands. Whoever does not take warning from others is taught a lesson in himself. And in the authentic proverbs: "The happy one is he who is admonished by others."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 59, verse 3–4:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And had it not been that Allah had decreed for them exile﴾. That is, had it not been that He had decreed that He would expel them from their homes, and that they would remain for a period, during which some of them would believe and children would be born to them who would believe.

﴿He would have punished them in this world﴾. That is, by killing and taking captive, as He did with the Banu Qurayzah. Al-Jala' (exile) is leaving one's homeland. It is said: jala bi-nafsihi jalaa'an (he departed of his own accord), and ajlahu ghayruhu ijlaa'an (another expelled him). The difference between al-Jala' and al-Ikhraj (expulsion), although their meaning in terms of removal is one, is in two respects. The first: al-Jala' is that which occurs together with one's family and children, whereas al-Ikhraj may occur while family and children remain. The second: al-Jala' occurs only to a group, whereas al-Ikhraj occurs to an individual or to a group. This was stated by al-Mawardi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That﴾, that is, that exile (is) ﴿because they opposed Allah﴾, that is, they were hostile to Him and defied His command.

﴿And whoever opposes Allah﴾. Talhah ibn Musarrif and Muhammad ibn al-Sumayfa' recited ﴿wa-man yushāqiq Allāh﴾ with the doubled consonant made explicit (wa-man yushāqiqi Allāh), as in the instance in "al-Anfal" [[See vol. 7, p. 379.]], while the rest assimilated (idghām) the doubling.

**First issue: the words of Allah, "Whatever palm trees you cut down..."**

In it are five issues.

**The first issue:** Allah's words ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down﴾. The word *ma* (whatever) is in the accusative position governed by *qataʿtum* (you cut down), as though he said: "What thing did you cut down?" The reason is that when the Prophet ﷺ came down upon the fortresses of Banu al-Nadir, which are al-Buwayra, after they broke the covenant by aiding Quraysh against him on the day of Uhud, he ordered that their palm trees be cut down and burned. They differed over the number of trees. Qatada and al-Dahhak said: they cut down and burned six palm trees. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: they cut down one palm tree and burned one palm tree. This was with the approval of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ or by his command, either to weaken them through it or for the sake of widening the space by cutting it down. This was grievous to them, and they said, and they were the Jews, the People of the Book: "O Muhammad, do you not claim that you are a Prophet who seeks righteousness? Is it righteousness to cut down palm trees and burn trees? Did you find in what Allah revealed to you permission for corruption on earth?" This was grievous to the Prophet ﷺ. The believers were troubled in their souls, to the point that they disagreed. Some of them said: "Do not cut down anything of what Allah has granted us as spoil." Others said: "Cut them down, so that we may enrage them by that." So the verse was revealed, confirming those who forbade the cutting, permitting the one who cut from sin, and informing that cutting and leaving it were by the permission of Allah.

Their poet, Simak the Jew, said regarding that:

*Did we not inherit the Wise Book*
*in the time of Moses, and we were not deceived?*

*And you are shepherds of goats, lean,*
*in the plain of Tihama and al-Akhyaf.*

*You see herding as glory for you,*
*in every age there is for you a ruinous [lot].*

*So O you witnesses, cease*
*from injustice and from the crooked speech.*

*Perhaps the nights and the turns of the ages*
*will bring down from the just, the equitable one*

*by the slaying of al-Nadir and their expulsion*
*[and their allies] and the felling of the palms, and they were not picked.*

Hassan ibn Thabit answered him:

*A group has made a covenant, who aided Quraysh,*
*and they have no helper in their own land.*

*They were given the Book and wasted it,*
*and they are blind to the Torah, destroyed.*

*You disbelieved in the Qur'an, and you refused*
*the confirmation of what the warner said.*

*And it was easy for the chiefs of the sons of Lu'ayy*
*that a spreading fire at al-Buwayra [burned].*

Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib answered him:

*May Allah perpetuate that deed,*
*and may the blaze burn in its regions.*

*You will know which of us will be there in the end,*
*and we will know which of our lands will be the destination.*

*Had the palms been there as camels for riding,*
*they would have said: "There is no staying for you, so depart."*

**The second issue:** The Prophet's ﷺ going out against them was in Rabi' al-Awwal, at the beginning of the fourth year after the Hijra. They fortified themselves against him in the fortresses. He ordered the palm trees cut down and burned. At that time the prohibition of wine was revealed. ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and those with him among the hypocrites sent to Banu al-Nadir: "We are with you; if you are fought, we will fight with you; if you are expelled, we will go out with you." So they were deceived by that. But when the reality came, they abandoned them, delivered them over, and laid down their arms. They asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to spare their lives and let them leave, on condition that they could take whatever their camels could carry of their wealth, except weapons. So they departed thus to Khaybar, and some of them went to Syria. Among those who went to Khaybar were their chiefs, such as Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Sallam ibn Abi al-Huqayq, and Kinana ibn al-Rabi'. Then Khaybar submitted to them.

**The third issue:** It is established in Sahih Muslim and other collections, from Ibn ʿUmar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ cut down the palm trees of Banu al-Nadir and burned them. And Hassan said concerning it:

*A spreading fire at al-Buwayra*
*was easy for the chiefs of the sons of Lu'ayy.*

And concerning that was revealed: ﴿Whatever palm trees you cut down﴾, to the end of the verse. People differed over the destruction of the enemy's house, its burning, and the cutting of its fruit-bearing trees, on two views. The first: that it is permissible, as stated in al-Mudawwana. The second: if the Muslims know that it will be theirs, they should not do it; and if they despair of that, they may do it, as Malik said in al-Wadiha. The companions of al-Shafiʿi debate according to this. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The correct view is the first. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ knew that the palm trees of Banu al-Nadir would be his, yet he cut them down and burned them so that this would be a harm to them and a weakening among them, until they left it. The destruction of part of property for the sake of the welfare of what remains is a permissible benefit in the Shariʿa and sound in reason.

**The fourth issue:** Al-Mawardi said: In this verse there is evidence that every mujtahid (one who exercises ijtihad, independent legal reasoning) is correct. This was also said by al-Kiya al-Tabari, who said: Although ijtihad is far-fetched in such a matter while the Prophet ﷺ was present among them, and there is no doubt that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw that and remained silent, so they took the ruling only from his tacit approval. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: This is false, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was with them, and there is no ijtihad in the presence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Rather, it indicates the ijtihad of the Prophet ﷺ in what had not been revealed to him, acting on the generality of the harm to the disbelievers, and entering into the permission given to all to bring about their annihilation and ruin. This is Allah's words: ﴿and that He may disgrace the defiantly disobedient﴾.

**The fifth issue:** There is disagreement about what *al-līna* (the palm trees) is, with ten views. The first: it is all palm trees except the ʿAjwa, said by al-Zuhri, Malik, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrima and al-Khalil. From Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan: it is all palm trees, and they did not exclude ʿAjwa or anything else. Also from Ibn ʿAbbas: it is a type of palm tree. From al-Thawri: it is the noble palm trees. From Abu ʿUbayda: it is all kinds of dates except the ʿAjwa and the Barni (Barni, with a fatha on the ba and a sukun on the ra: a kind of date, reddish tinged with yellow, with much fibre, sweet in flavour).

Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad said: it is specifically the ʿAjwa. It is mentioned that the ʿAtiq and the ʿAjwa were with Noah, peace be upon him, in the ark. The ʿAtiq is the male. The ʿAjwa was the origin of all the female palms, and therefore it was grievous to the Jews to cut it down, related by al-Mawardi. It is also said: it is a kind of palm tree whose dates are called *al-lawn*; its dates are the finest of dates, very yellow, its pit can be seen from outside, and the molar sinks into it. A single palm of it is dearer to them than a servant (*wasif*: a servant, whether male or female).

It is also said: it is the palm tree close to the ground. Al-Akhfash recited:

*The dove has saddened me when it sang*
*with the separation of loved ones, from above the palm of līna.*

It is also said: *al-līna* is the young shoot, because it is softer than the palm tree. From this is the poet's saying:

*They planted its līna by the course of Maʿin,*
*then they surrounded the palms with the thickets.*

It is also said: *al-līna* is all trees, because of their softness with life. Dhu al-Rumma said:

*The covering of the flight feathers falls upon a līna,*
*the dew of its night glistening on its plumage.*

The tenth view: it is the inferior date (*daqal*), said by al-Asmaʿi. He said: The people of Medina say: the tables are not filled until the varieties are found, meaning the daqal. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: The correct view is what al-Zuhri and Malik said, for two reasons. The first: they are the best informed about their land and its trees. The second: the derivation supports it, and the linguists confirm it. The word *līna* has the form *lūna*, and it was made defective on their principles, so it became *līna*, and thus it is *lawn*. When the ha' is added, its first letter is kasra, like *barkih al-ṣadr* (with fatha on the ba) and *birkih* (with kasra), because of the ha'. It is also said: *līna* originally was *lūna*, and the waw was changed to ya' because of the kasra before it. The plural of *līna* is *līn*. It is also said: *liyān*. Imru' al-Qays, describing the neck of his horse, said:

*And a neck like the palm-fibres of the līyān,*
*in which the blazing fire has kindled.*

Al-Akhfash said: It was named *līna* by derivation from *lawn* (colour), not from *layn* (softness). Al-Mahdawi said: Its derivation is disputed. It is said: it is from *lawn*, and its origin is *lūna*. It is also said its origin is *līna*, from *lāna yalīnu*. ʿAbd Allah recited: "Whatever palm trees you cut down, and what you left standing upon their roots" (*qawmāʾa*), meaning standing upon their trunks. Al-Aʿmash recited: "Whatever palm trees you cut down or left them standing (*qawman*) upon their roots," meaning: you did not cut them down. It was also read: "*qawmāʾa ʿalā uṣulihā*." In this there are two views: the first, that it is the plural of *aṣl* (root), like *rahn* and *ruhun*. The second: the damma is sufficient instead of the waw. It was also read: "*qāʾiman ʿalā uṣūlihi*," going back to the wording of *mā* (whatever).

**"By the permission of Allah"**, that is, by His command. **"And that He may disgrace the defiantly disobedient"**, that is, that He may humiliate the Jewish disbelievers by it, and by His Messenger and His Books.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 59, verse 6–7 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from them﴾. This verse and the one after it, up to His saying ﴿severe in punishment﴾ [the text between the two brackets is missing from manuscripts ḥ and s], contain ten issues.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever Allah restored (afāʾa) to His Messenger﴾, meaning what Allah, Exalted is He, returned to His Messenger from the property of the Banu al-Nadir. ﴿Then you did not spur upon it (fa-mā awjaftum ʿalayhi)﴾, that is, you did not hasten toward it. Al-Ījāf is al-īḍāʿ (urging on) in travel, which is haste. It is said: "wajafa al-faras" when the horse hastened, and "awjaftuhu" means I set it in motion and tired it. From this is the saying of Tamim ibn Muqbil:

Mudhāwīd bi-l-bīḍ al-ḥadīth ṣiqāluhā... ʿan al-rakb aḥyānan idhā al-rakb awjafū

And al-rikāb are camels, its singular being rāḥilah. The meaning is: you did not cover a distance to reach it, nor did you encounter in it war or hardship, for it was two miles from Medina, as stated by al-Farrāʾ. So they walked to it on foot and did not ride horses or camels, except the Prophet ﷺ, who rode a camel, and it is said a donkey, with a halter of palm fibre. He conquered it by treaty, expelled them, and took their property. The Muslims asked the Prophet ﷺ to distribute it among them, and so this was revealed: ﴿And whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from them, you did not spur upon it﴾, the verse. Thus the property of the Banu al-Nadir was made exclusively for the Prophet ﷺ, to place wherever he wished, and the Prophet ﷺ distributed it among the Emigrants (al-Muhājirūn). Al-Waqidi said: Ibn Wahb narrated it from Malik, and he gave none of it to the Helpers (al-Anṣār) except three men in need: among them Abu Dujana Simak ibn Kharasha, Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, and al-Ḥarith ibn al-Ṣimma. It is also said that he gave to only two men, Sahl and Abu Dujana. It is said he gave Saʿd ibn Muʿadh the sword of Ibn Abi al-Ḥuqayq, which had a reputation among them. And none of the Banu al-Nadir became Muslim except two men: Sufyan ibn ʿUmayr and Saʿd ibn Wahb, who embraced Islam while retaining their property, and so they secured it.

In the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, from ʿUmar, who said: The property of the Banu al-Nadir was among what Allah restored to His Messenger, which the Muslims had not spurred upon with horses or camels, and it was exclusively for the Prophet ﷺ. He would spend on his family a year's provision, and what remained he would put into the horses and weapons (al-kurāʿ [the animals fit for war]) as preparation in the way of Allah, Exalted is He. Al-ʿAbbas said to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them: Judge between me and this lying, sinful, treacherous, deceitful man, meaning ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning what Allah restored to His Messenger from the property of the Banu al-Nadir. ʿUmar said: Do you both know that the Prophet ﷺ said: "We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity"? They said: Yes. ʿUmar said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had specially favoured His Messenger ﷺ with something and had not singled out anyone else with it. He said: ﴿Whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns, it is for Allah and for the Messenger﴾ (I do not know whether he recited the verse before it or not). So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ distributed among you the property of the Banu al-Nadir. By Allah, he did not keep it to himself over you, nor did he take it to the exclusion of you, until this property remained, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would take from it a year's provision, then he would put what remained as the common share of the wealth... the hadith in its entirety, related by Muslim.

It is also said: When the Banu al-Nadir left their homes and property, the Muslims asked that they have a share in it like the spoils of war. Then Allah, Exalted is He, made clear that it belonged... And there had occurred some fighting there, for they were besieged for days, and they fought and some were killed, then they made peace on the condition of exile. There was no real fighting, rather the beginnings of fighting occurred and a siege took place, and Allah specified those properties for His Messenger ﷺ. Mujahid said: Allah informed them and reminded them that He had only given victory to His Messenger ﷺ, and had given them victory without equipment or preparation.

﴿But Allah gives His messengers power over whomever He wills﴾, that is, over His enemies. In this is a clarification that those properties were exclusively for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, not for his companions.

The second: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: They are Qurayza and al-Nadir, and both are in Medina, and Fadak, which is three days from Medina, and Khaybar. The villages of ʿUrayna and Yanbuʿ, Allah made them for His Messenger. He made clear that in that property which He specified for the Messenger, peace be upon him, there are shares for others than the Messenger, out of His consideration for His servants. The scholars have spoken about this verse and the one before it: is their meaning one or different? The verse in al-Anfal... Some scholars said: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾ is abrogated (mansūkh) by what is in Sūrat al-Anfāl concerning the fifth (al-khums) being for those named, and the four remaining fifths for those who fought. In the early period of Islam the spoils were divided among these categories, and there was nothing for those who fought for them. This is the view of Yazid ibn Rumān, Qatada and others, and similar is reported from Malik. Others said: It was obtained by treaty without the spurring of horses or camels, so it belongs to those whom Allah named in it as fay'. The first share is for the Prophet ﷺ exclusively; when he took his need from it, the remainder was for the public interests of the Muslims. Maʿmar said: The first (verse) is for the Prophet ﷺ; the second is the jizya and kharāj for the categories mentioned in it; the third is the spoils in Sūrat al-Anfāl for the warriors who gained them.

Others, among them al-Shafiʿi, said: The meaning of the two verses is one, that is, what was obtained from the property of the disbelievers without fighting is divided into five shares, four of which are for the Prophet ﷺ. The remaining fifth is divided into five shares: one share for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as well, one for the kinsfolk (dhawī al-qurbā), who are the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, because they were denied zakat, so a right in the fay' was given to them; one for the orphans; one for the needy; and one for the wayfarer (ibn al-sabīl). As for after the death of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, what was of the fay' belonging to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is, according to al-Shafiʿi in one view, spent on the fighters stationed at the frontiers, because they stand in the place of the Messenger, peace be upon him. In another of his views, it is spent on the public interests of the Muslims, such as sealing the frontiers, digging canals, and building bridges, with the most important given priority. This applies to four-fifths of the fay'. As for the share which was his from the fifth of the fay' and the spoils, it is for the public interests of the Muslims after his death, without disagreement, as he, peace be upon him, said: "I have no share of your spoils except the fifth, and the fifth is returned to you." This matter was discussed in Sūrat al-Anfāl [see vol. 8, p. 11]. Likewise, what he left of property is not inherited, but is charity, spent on the public interests of the Muslims, as he, peace be upon him, said: "We do not inherit; what we leave is charity." It is also said: The property of the fay' belonged to his Prophet ﷺ, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿what Allah restored to His Messenger﴾, attributing it to him, except that he did not accumulate wealth (al-mutaʾaththil [the one who accumulates]); he only took according to the need of his dependants and spent the rest on the public interests of the Muslims. Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: There is no difficulty that these are three meanings in three verses. As for the first verse, it is His saying: ﴿He it is who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 2], then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And what Allah restored to His Messenger from them﴾, meaning from the People of the Book, joined to them.

﴿So you did not spur upon it, of horses or camels﴾: he means, as we have explained, that you have no right to it. For this reason ʿUmar said: It was exclusively for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, meaning the Banu al-Nadir and what was like it. This is one verse and one meaning. The second verse: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns, it is for Allah and for the Messenger﴾, and this is a separate statement from the first, for a different recipient from the first. He called the third verse the verse of the spoils (āyat al-ghanīma). There is no doubt that it is another meaning, with a second entitlement for another recipient. However, the first and second verses share that each of them included something Allah restored to His Messenger, and the first verse implied that it was obtained without fighting, while the verse of al-Anfal implied that it was obtained by fighting. The third verse, His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾, is free of mention of whether it was obtained by fighting or without fighting, and so the disagreement arose here. One group said: it is attached to the first, which is the entire property of treaty and the like. Another group said: it is attached to the second, which is the verse of al-Anfal. Those who said it is attached to the verse of al-Anfal disagreed: is it abrogated, as has passed, or muḥkam (firm, not abrogated)? Attaching it to Allah's testimony to the one before it is better, because it renews a benefit and meaning. It is known that carrying a letter of the verse, let alone the verse, to a renewed benefit is better than carrying it to a repeated benefit. Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So you did not spur upon it, of horses or camels﴾ — the Banu al-Nadir — there was no fifth in it, and it was not spurred upon with horses or camels. It was purely for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he divided it among the Emigrants and three men of the Helpers, as previously mentioned. His saying: ﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾ refers to Qurayza, and Qurayza and the Trench were on one day. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: Malik's statement that the second verse is about the Banu Qurayza indicates that its meaning returns to the verse of al-Anfal, and abrogation applies to it. This is stronger than the view of its being firm. We choose only what we have divided and clarified: that the second verse has a renewed meaning, according to what we have shown. And Allah knows best.

I say: What he chose is good. It has been said that Sūrat al-Ḥashr was revealed after al-Anfal, and it is impossible that the earlier abrogate the later. Ibn Abi Najih said: Property is of three kinds: spoils (maghnam), fay', or charity (ṣadaqa), and there is not a single dirham of it but Allah has made clear its place. This is more likely.

The third: The properties that come under the control of imams and rulers have three kinds of entry. The first: what is taken from Muslims as a means of purifying them, such as ṣadaqāt and zakāt. The second: the spoils (ghanāʾim), which is what comes into the hands of the Muslims from the property of the disbelievers by war, conquest, and victory. The third: the fay', which is what returns to the Muslims from the property of the disbelievers without fighting or spurring, such as treaty payments, the jizya, the kharāj, and the ʿushr taken from the disbelieving merchants. Similar is when polytheists flee and leave their property, or when one of them dies in the abode of Islam with no heir. As for ṣadaqa, its recipients are the poor, the needy, and those who work on it, as Allah mentioned, and this has passed in Sūrat Barāʾa [see vol. 8, p. 67]. As for the spoils, they were

In the early days of Islam, the Prophet ﷺ would dispose of it as he wished, as he said in Surah al-Anfal: ﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: the spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 1]. Then it was abrogated (naskh) by His saying, ﴿And know that whatever you take as booty (ghanima)...﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], to the end of the verse. Its explanation has already passed in al-Anfal [see vol. 8, p. 9].

As for the fay' (wealth acquired from the enemy without fighting), its division and the division of the one-fifth (khumus) are the same. According to Malik, the decision about both rests with the imam. If he sees fit to withhold them for calamities that befall the Muslims, he may do so. If he sees fit to distribute them, or to distribute one of them, he distributes all of it among the people, equally between their Arabs and their clients (mawali). He begins with the poor, men and women, until they become wealthy. The relatives of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ are given their share of the fay' as the imam sees fit, and there is no fixed limit for this.

Scholars differed on giving to the wealthy among them. Most people held that it is given to them, because it is their right. Malik said: only their poor are given from it, because it was made for them as a substitute for zakat. Al-Shafi'i said: whatever wealth of the unbelievers is obtained without fighting was divided in the time of the Prophet ﷺ into twenty-five shares: twenty for the Prophet ﷺ, who would do with them as he wished, and the khumus, which is divided in the same way as the khumus of the ghanima. Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn al-Dawudi said: this is an opinion that no one we know of preceded him in holding. Rather, that was exclusively his, as is established in the Sahih from Umar, who explained the verse. Had this been the case, His saying, ﴿exclusively for you, apart from the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50], would indicate that the gift may be granted to others, and His saying, ﴿exclusively for them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-A'raf: 32], would permit others to share in it with them. Al-Shafi'i's view has already been discussed in full on this, praise be to Allah.

The position of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, is that the way of the khumus of the fay' is the way of the khumus of the ghanima, and that four-fifths of it belonged to the Prophet ﷺ, and after him it is for the interests of the Muslims. He has another view: that after him it belongs to those who dedicate themselves to fighting after him, exclusively, as was mentioned earlier.

Fourth: Our scholars said: every wealth is distributed in the town where it was collected, and it is not transferred from that town until its people become wealthy. Then it is moved to the nearest of others, unless a severe hardship befalls people outside the town where it was collected, in which case it is transferred to the people in hardship wherever they are, as Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, did in the Year of Ashes (amwas al-Ramada), which lasted five or six years. It has also been said that it lasted two years, and it has been said: a year in which the plague grew severe along with hunger.

If none of what we have described applies and the imam sees fit to hold the fay' in reserve, he holds it for the calamities of the Muslims. He gives from it to the newborn, and begins with the one whose father is poor. The fay' is lawful for the wealthy. He equalizes people in it, except that he gives preference to those in need and hardship. The preference in it is only according to the degree of need. Debtors are given from it what they need to pay their debts. He gives from it prizes and gifts if they are deserving, and he provides for judges, rulers, and whoever is of benefit to the Muslims. Those with the greatest share of it are those most beneficial to the Muslims.

Whoever takes something of the fay' from the register (diwan) is obligated to go on raids when raids are conducted.

Fifth: His saying, ﴿so that it does not become a circulating commodity among the rich among you﴾. The common reading is yakuna with the "ya" and dawlatan in the accusative, meaning: so that the fay' does not become a circulating commodity. Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Hisham (from Ibn Amir), and Abu Haywa read "takuna" with the "ta," and dawlatun in the nominative, meaning: so that a circulating commodity does not occur. Here "kana" is complete (tamma), and dawlatun is the subject of kana with no predicate. It is also possible that kana is incomplete (naqisa), with its predicate being "among the rich among you." When it is complete, His saying "among the rich among you" is connected to dawlatan in the sense of "circulating among the rich among you." It is also possible that "among the rich among you" is a qualifier of dawlatan. The common reading is dawlatan with a damma on the dal. Al-Sulami and Abu Haywa read it in the accusative.

Isa ibn Umar, Yunus, and al-Asma'i said: the two are dialects with the same meaning. Abu Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: al-dawla (with a fatha) is victory in war and other things, and it is the verbal noun. With a damma, it is the name of what circulates among wealth. Abu Ubayda likewise said: al-dawla is the name of the thing that circulates, and al-dawla (with a fatha) is the act.

The meaning of the verse is: We did this with this fay' so that its leaders, rich and powerful, do not divide it among themselves to the exclusion of the poor and weak. For the people of the Jahiliyya, when they seized booty, the chief would take a quarter of it for himself, which was the mirba'. Then after the mirba', he would also select whatever he wished. Their poet said about this:

"For you is the quarter of it, and the choice portions,
and your judgment, and the nashita, and the fudul."

He says: so that it is not handled as it was handled in the Jahiliyya. Allah therefore assigned this to His Messenger ﷺ, to distribute it in the places He commanded, and there was no khumus in it. When a khumus came, it fell among all the Muslims.

Sixth: His saying, ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾. That is, whatever he gives you of the spoils of war, take it; and whatever he forbids you from taking or from ghulul (embezzlement from the spoils, theft from the booty), refrain from it. This was said by al-Hasan and others. Al-Suddi said: whatever he gives you from the fay' wealth, accept it, and whatever he withholds from you, do not seek it. Ibn Jurayj said: whatever he commands you of my obedience, do it, and whatever he forbids you of my disobedience, avoid it. Al-Mawardi said: it has also been said that it applies generally to all his commands and prohibitions: he commands only what is good and forbids only what is corrupt. I say: this is the meaning of the view before it. So there are three views.

Seventh: Al-Mahdawi said regarding His saying, ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾: this necessitates that everything the Prophet ﷺ commands is a command from Allah the Exalted. Although the verse concerns the spoils, all his commands and prohibitions, ﷺ, are included in it. Al-Hakam ibn Umayr, who had companionship with the Prophet ﷺ, said: the Prophet ﷺ said: "This Qur'an is difficult and hard to grasp, arduous for one who abandons it, and easy for one who follows and seeks it. My hadith is also difficult and hard to grasp, and it is the judgment. Whoever holds fast to my hadith and memorizes it will be saved along with the Qur'an. Whoever takes the Qur'an and my hadith lightly will lose this world and the Hereafter. You are commanded to take up my words, to surround my affair, and to follow my sunna. Whoever is content with my words has been content with the Qur'an, and whoever mocks my words has mocked the Qur'an." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾.

Eighth: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: Ibn Mas'ud met a man in the state of ihram wearing his clothes, and he said to him: "Take that off." The man said: "Are you reciting to me a verse from the Book of Allah?" He said: "Yes: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾." Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Harun al-Firyabi said: I heard al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, say: "Ask me about whatever you wish, and I will inform you from the Book of Allah and the sunna of your Prophet ﷺ." He said: I asked him, "What do you say, may Allah set you right, about the muhrim who kills a wasp?" He said: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾."

Sufyan ibn Uyayna narrated to us from Abd al-Malik ibn Umayr, from Ribi ibn Hirash, from Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Follow the two after me, Abu Bakr and Umar." Sufyan ibn Uyayna narrated to us from Mis'ar ibn Kidam, from Qays ibn Muslim, from Tariq ibn Shihab, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he commanded the killing of the wasp.

Our scholars said: this is an answer of the utmost excellence. He issued a legal ruling permitting the killing of a wasp during ihram, and clarified that one follows Umar in this, and that the Prophet ﷺ commanded following him, and that Allah the Exalted commanded accepting what the Prophet ﷺ says. Therefore the permissibility of killing it is derived from the Book and the Sunna. This same meaning has already passed from the statement of Ikrima when he was asked about umm al-walad (slave-mothers), and he said: "They are free," in Surah al-Nisa, at His saying: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾ [al-Nisa: 59] [see vol. 5, pp. 259 and 392].

In Sahih Muslim and elsewhere, from Alqama, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah has cursed the women who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, the women who pluck their facial hair (mutanammisat), the women who file their teeth to appear beautiful (mutafalijat), and those who alter the creation of Allah." [Mutanammisat: those who pluck hair from their faces. Mutafalijat: those who take pains to create gaps between their front teeth and molars.] This reached a woman from the Banu Asad called Umm Ya'qub. She came and said: "I have heard that you cursed such and such!" He said: "Why should I not curse one whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed, and it is in the Book of Allah!" She said: "I have read everything between the two covers and found nothing in it of what you say." He said: "If you had read it, you would have found it! Have you not read: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾?" She said: "Yes." He said: "He has forbidden it..." (the hadith). The matter has already been discussed fully in al-Nisa [see vol. 5, pp. 259 and 392].

Ninth: His saying, ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾. Although it comes with the wording "giving" (itaʼ), which means handing over, its meaning is a command. This is shown by His saying, ﴿and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾, pairing it with the prohibition, and a prohibition is only paired with a command. The proof for understanding this is what we mentioned before, along with the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, peace be upon him: "If I command you to do something, do of it what you are able; and if I forbid you from something, avoid it."

Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning the leaders of the Muslims. They said, regarding the wealth of the polytheists that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had seized: "O Messenger of Allah, take your choice portion (safi) and the quarter, and leave us the rest, for this is how we used to do it in the Jahiliyya." And they recited to him:

"For you is the quarter of it, and the choice portions,
and your judgment, and the nashita, and the fudul."

So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Tenth: His saying, ﴿And fear Allah﴾, that is, the punishment of Allah, for His punishment is severe for whoever disobeys Him. It has also been said: fear Allah regarding His commands and prohibitions, so do not neglect them.

﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾ for whoever opposes what He has commanded him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 59, verse 6–7 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from them﴾. This verse and the one after it, up to His saying ﴿severe in punishment﴾ [the text between the two brackets is missing from manuscripts ḥ and s], contain ten issues.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whatever Allah restored (afāʾa) to His Messenger﴾, meaning what Allah, Exalted is He, returned to His Messenger from the property of the Banu al-Nadir. ﴿Then you did not spur upon it (fa-mā awjaftum ʿalayhi)﴾, that is, you did not hasten toward it. Al-Ījāf is al-īḍāʿ (urging on) in travel, which is haste. It is said: "wajafa al-faras" when the horse hastened, and "awjaftuhu" means I set it in motion and tired it. From this is the saying of Tamim ibn Muqbil:

Mudhāwīd bi-l-bīḍ al-ḥadīth ṣiqāluhā... ʿan al-rakb aḥyānan idhā al-rakb awjafū

And al-rikāb are camels, its singular being rāḥilah. The meaning is: you did not cover a distance to reach it, nor did you encounter in it war or hardship, for it was two miles from Medina, as stated by al-Farrāʾ. So they walked to it on foot and did not ride horses or camels, except the Prophet ﷺ, who rode a camel, and it is said a donkey, with a halter of palm fibre. He conquered it by treaty, expelled them, and took their property. The Muslims asked the Prophet ﷺ to distribute it among them, and so this was revealed: ﴿And whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from them, you did not spur upon it﴾, the verse. Thus the property of the Banu al-Nadir was made exclusively for the Prophet ﷺ, to place wherever he wished, and the Prophet ﷺ distributed it among the Emigrants (al-Muhājirūn). Al-Waqidi said: Ibn Wahb narrated it from Malik, and he gave none of it to the Helpers (al-Anṣār) except three men in need: among them Abu Dujana Simak ibn Kharasha, Sahl ibn Ḥunayf, and al-Ḥarith ibn al-Ṣimma. It is also said that he gave to only two men, Sahl and Abu Dujana. It is said he gave Saʿd ibn Muʿadh the sword of Ibn Abi al-Ḥuqayq, which had a reputation among them. And none of the Banu al-Nadir became Muslim except two men: Sufyan ibn ʿUmayr and Saʿd ibn Wahb, who embraced Islam while retaining their property, and so they secured it.

In the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, from ʿUmar, who said: The property of the Banu al-Nadir was among what Allah restored to His Messenger, which the Muslims had not spurred upon with horses or camels, and it was exclusively for the Prophet ﷺ. He would spend on his family a year's provision, and what remained he would put into the horses and weapons (al-kurāʿ [the animals fit for war]) as preparation in the way of Allah, Exalted is He. Al-ʿAbbas said to ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them: Judge between me and this lying, sinful, treacherous, deceitful man, meaning ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning what Allah restored to His Messenger from the property of the Banu al-Nadir. ʿUmar said: Do you both know that the Prophet ﷺ said: "We do not leave inheritance; what we leave is charity"? They said: Yes. ʿUmar said: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had specially favoured His Messenger ﷺ with something and had not singled out anyone else with it. He said: ﴿Whatever Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns, it is for Allah and for the Messenger﴾ (I do not know whether he recited the verse before it or not). So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ distributed among you the property of the Banu al-Nadir. By Allah, he did not keep it to himself over you, nor did he take it to the exclusion of you, until this property remained, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would take from it a year's provision, then he would put what remained as the common share of the wealth... the hadith in its entirety, related by Muslim.

It is also said: When the Banu al-Nadir left their homes and property, the Muslims asked that they have a share in it like the spoils of war. Then Allah, Exalted is He, made clear that it belonged... And there had occurred some fighting there, for they were besieged for days, and they fought and some were killed, then they made peace on the condition of exile. There was no real fighting, rather the beginnings of fighting occurred and a siege took place, and Allah specified those properties for His Messenger ﷺ. Mujahid said: Allah informed them and reminded them that He had only given victory to His Messenger ﷺ, and had given them victory without equipment or preparation.

﴿But Allah gives His messengers power over whomever He wills﴾, that is, over His enemies. In this is a clarification that those properties were exclusively for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, not for his companions.

The second: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: They are Qurayza and al-Nadir, and both are in Medina, and Fadak, which is three days from Medina, and Khaybar. The villages of ʿUrayna and Yanbuʿ, Allah made them for His Messenger. He made clear that in that property which He specified for the Messenger, peace be upon him, there are shares for others than the Messenger, out of His consideration for His servants. The scholars have spoken about this verse and the one before it: is their meaning one or different? The verse in al-Anfal... Some scholars said: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾ is abrogated (mansūkh) by what is in Sūrat al-Anfāl concerning the fifth (al-khums) being for those named, and the four remaining fifths for those who fought. In the early period of Islam the spoils were divided among these categories, and there was nothing for those who fought for them. This is the view of Yazid ibn Rumān, Qatada and others, and similar is reported from Malik. Others said: It was obtained by treaty without the spurring of horses or camels, so it belongs to those whom Allah named in it as fay'. The first share is for the Prophet ﷺ exclusively; when he took his need from it, the remainder was for the public interests of the Muslims. Maʿmar said: The first (verse) is for the Prophet ﷺ; the second is the jizya and kharāj for the categories mentioned in it; the third is the spoils in Sūrat al-Anfāl for the warriors who gained them.

Others, among them al-Shafiʿi, said: The meaning of the two verses is one, that is, what was obtained from the property of the disbelievers without fighting is divided into five shares, four of which are for the Prophet ﷺ. The remaining fifth is divided into five shares: one share for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ as well, one for the kinsfolk (dhawī al-qurbā), who are the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib, because they were denied zakat, so a right in the fay' was given to them; one for the orphans; one for the needy; and one for the wayfarer (ibn al-sabīl). As for after the death of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, what was of the fay' belonging to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is, according to al-Shafiʿi in one view, spent on the fighters stationed at the frontiers, because they stand in the place of the Messenger, peace be upon him. In another of his views, it is spent on the public interests of the Muslims, such as sealing the frontiers, digging canals, and building bridges, with the most important given priority. This applies to four-fifths of the fay'. As for the share which was his from the fifth of the fay' and the spoils, it is for the public interests of the Muslims after his death, without disagreement, as he, peace be upon him, said: "I have no share of your spoils except the fifth, and the fifth is returned to you." This matter was discussed in Sūrat al-Anfāl [see vol. 8, p. 11]. Likewise, what he left of property is not inherited, but is charity, spent on the public interests of the Muslims, as he, peace be upon him, said: "We do not inherit; what we leave is charity." It is also said: The property of the fay' belonged to his Prophet ﷺ, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿what Allah restored to His Messenger﴾, attributing it to him, except that he did not accumulate wealth (al-mutaʾaththil [the one who accumulates]); he only took according to the need of his dependants and spent the rest on the public interests of the Muslims. Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi said: There is no difficulty that these are three meanings in three verses. As for the first verse, it is His saying: ﴿He it is who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering﴾ [al-Ḥashr: 2], then He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And what Allah restored to His Messenger from them﴾, meaning from the People of the Book, joined to them.

﴿So you did not spur upon it, of horses or camels﴾: he means, as we have explained, that you have no right to it. For this reason ʿUmar said: It was exclusively for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, meaning the Banu al-Nadir and what was like it. This is one verse and one meaning. The second verse: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns, it is for Allah and for the Messenger﴾, and this is a separate statement from the first, for a different recipient from the first. He called the third verse the verse of the spoils (āyat al-ghanīma). There is no doubt that it is another meaning, with a second entitlement for another recipient. However, the first and second verses share that each of them included something Allah restored to His Messenger, and the first verse implied that it was obtained without fighting, while the verse of al-Anfal implied that it was obtained by fighting. The third verse, His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾, is free of mention of whether it was obtained by fighting or without fighting, and so the disagreement arose here. One group said: it is attached to the first, which is the entire property of treaty and the like. Another group said: it is attached to the second, which is the verse of al-Anfal. Those who said it is attached to the verse of al-Anfal disagreed: is it abrogated, as has passed, or muḥkam (firm, not abrogated)? Attaching it to Allah's testimony to the one before it is better, because it renews a benefit and meaning. It is known that carrying a letter of the verse, let alone the verse, to a renewed benefit is better than carrying it to a repeated benefit. Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So you did not spur upon it, of horses or camels﴾ — the Banu al-Nadir — there was no fifth in it, and it was not spurred upon with horses or camels. It was purely for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he divided it among the Emigrants and three men of the Helpers, as previously mentioned. His saying: ﴿What Allah restored to His Messenger from the people of the towns﴾ refers to Qurayza, and Qurayza and the Trench were on one day. Ibn al-ʿArabi said: Malik's statement that the second verse is about the Banu Qurayza indicates that its meaning returns to the verse of al-Anfal, and abrogation applies to it. This is stronger than the view of its being firm. We choose only what we have divided and clarified: that the second verse has a renewed meaning, according to what we have shown. And Allah knows best.

I say: What he chose is good. It has been said that Sūrat al-Ḥashr was revealed after al-Anfal, and it is impossible that the earlier abrogate the later. Ibn Abi Najih said: Property is of three kinds: spoils (maghnam), fay', or charity (ṣadaqa), and there is not a single dirham of it but Allah has made clear its place. This is more likely.

The third: The properties that come under the control of imams and rulers have three kinds of entry. The first: what is taken from Muslims as a means of purifying them, such as ṣadaqāt and zakāt. The second: the spoils (ghanāʾim), which is what comes into the hands of the Muslims from the property of the disbelievers by war, conquest, and victory. The third: the fay', which is what returns to the Muslims from the property of the disbelievers without fighting or spurring, such as treaty payments, the jizya, the kharāj, and the ʿushr taken from the disbelieving merchants. Similar is when polytheists flee and leave their property, or when one of them dies in the abode of Islam with no heir. As for ṣadaqa, its recipients are the poor, the needy, and those who work on it, as Allah mentioned, and this has passed in Sūrat Barāʾa [see vol. 8, p. 67]. As for the spoils, they were

In the early days of Islam, the Prophet ﷺ would dispose of it as he wished, as he said in Surah al-Anfal: ﴿They ask you about the spoils. Say: the spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 1]. Then it was abrogated (naskh) by His saying, ﴿And know that whatever you take as booty (ghanima)...﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], to the end of the verse. Its explanation has already passed in al-Anfal [see vol. 8, p. 9].

As for the fay' (wealth acquired from the enemy without fighting), its division and the division of the one-fifth (khumus) are the same. According to Malik, the decision about both rests with the imam. If he sees fit to withhold them for calamities that befall the Muslims, he may do so. If he sees fit to distribute them, or to distribute one of them, he distributes all of it among the people, equally between their Arabs and their clients (mawali). He begins with the poor, men and women, until they become wealthy. The relatives of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ are given their share of the fay' as the imam sees fit, and there is no fixed limit for this.

Scholars differed on giving to the wealthy among them. Most people held that it is given to them, because it is their right. Malik said: only their poor are given from it, because it was made for them as a substitute for zakat. Al-Shafi'i said: whatever wealth of the unbelievers is obtained without fighting was divided in the time of the Prophet ﷺ into twenty-five shares: twenty for the Prophet ﷺ, who would do with them as he wished, and the khumus, which is divided in the same way as the khumus of the ghanima. Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn al-Dawudi said: this is an opinion that no one we know of preceded him in holding. Rather, that was exclusively his, as is established in the Sahih from Umar, who explained the verse. Had this been the case, His saying, ﴿exclusively for you, apart from the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50], would indicate that the gift may be granted to others, and His saying, ﴿exclusively for them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-A'raf: 32], would permit others to share in it with them. Al-Shafi'i's view has already been discussed in full on this, praise be to Allah.

The position of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, is that the way of the khumus of the fay' is the way of the khumus of the ghanima, and that four-fifths of it belonged to the Prophet ﷺ, and after him it is for the interests of the Muslims. He has another view: that after him it belongs to those who dedicate themselves to fighting after him, exclusively, as was mentioned earlier.

Fourth: Our scholars said: every wealth is distributed in the town where it was collected, and it is not transferred from that town until its people become wealthy. Then it is moved to the nearest of others, unless a severe hardship befalls people outside the town where it was collected, in which case it is transferred to the people in hardship wherever they are, as Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, did in the Year of Ashes (amwas al-Ramada), which lasted five or six years. It has also been said that it lasted two years, and it has been said: a year in which the plague grew severe along with hunger.

If none of what we have described applies and the imam sees fit to hold the fay' in reserve, he holds it for the calamities of the Muslims. He gives from it to the newborn, and begins with the one whose father is poor. The fay' is lawful for the wealthy. He equalizes people in it, except that he gives preference to those in need and hardship. The preference in it is only according to the degree of need. Debtors are given from it what they need to pay their debts. He gives from it prizes and gifts if they are deserving, and he provides for judges, rulers, and whoever is of benefit to the Muslims. Those with the greatest share of it are those most beneficial to the Muslims.

Whoever takes something of the fay' from the register (diwan) is obligated to go on raids when raids are conducted.

Fifth: His saying, ﴿so that it does not become a circulating commodity among the rich among you﴾. The common reading is yakuna with the "ya" and dawlatan in the accusative, meaning: so that the fay' does not become a circulating commodity. Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, Hisham (from Ibn Amir), and Abu Haywa read "takuna" with the "ta," and dawlatun in the nominative, meaning: so that a circulating commodity does not occur. Here "kana" is complete (tamma), and dawlatun is the subject of kana with no predicate. It is also possible that kana is incomplete (naqisa), with its predicate being "among the rich among you." When it is complete, His saying "among the rich among you" is connected to dawlatan in the sense of "circulating among the rich among you." It is also possible that "among the rich among you" is a qualifier of dawlatan. The common reading is dawlatan with a damma on the dal. Al-Sulami and Abu Haywa read it in the accusative.

Isa ibn Umar, Yunus, and al-Asma'i said: the two are dialects with the same meaning. Abu Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: al-dawla (with a fatha) is victory in war and other things, and it is the verbal noun. With a damma, it is the name of what circulates among wealth. Abu Ubayda likewise said: al-dawla is the name of the thing that circulates, and al-dawla (with a fatha) is the act.

The meaning of the verse is: We did this with this fay' so that its leaders, rich and powerful, do not divide it among themselves to the exclusion of the poor and weak. For the people of the Jahiliyya, when they seized booty, the chief would take a quarter of it for himself, which was the mirba'. Then after the mirba', he would also select whatever he wished. Their poet said about this:

"For you is the quarter of it, and the choice portions,
and your judgment, and the nashita, and the fudul."

He says: so that it is not handled as it was handled in the Jahiliyya. Allah therefore assigned this to His Messenger ﷺ, to distribute it in the places He commanded, and there was no khumus in it. When a khumus came, it fell among all the Muslims.

Sixth: His saying, ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾. That is, whatever he gives you of the spoils of war, take it; and whatever he forbids you from taking or from ghulul (embezzlement from the spoils, theft from the booty), refrain from it. This was said by al-Hasan and others. Al-Suddi said: whatever he gives you from the fay' wealth, accept it, and whatever he withholds from you, do not seek it. Ibn Jurayj said: whatever he commands you of my obedience, do it, and whatever he forbids you of my disobedience, avoid it. Al-Mawardi said: it has also been said that it applies generally to all his commands and prohibitions: he commands only what is good and forbids only what is corrupt. I say: this is the meaning of the view before it. So there are three views.

Seventh: Al-Mahdawi said regarding His saying, ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾: this necessitates that everything the Prophet ﷺ commands is a command from Allah the Exalted. Although the verse concerns the spoils, all his commands and prohibitions, ﷺ, are included in it. Al-Hakam ibn Umayr, who had companionship with the Prophet ﷺ, said: the Prophet ﷺ said: "This Qur'an is difficult and hard to grasp, arduous for one who abandons it, and easy for one who follows and seeks it. My hadith is also difficult and hard to grasp, and it is the judgment. Whoever holds fast to my hadith and memorizes it will be saved along with the Qur'an. Whoever takes the Qur'an and my hadith lightly will lose this world and the Hereafter. You are commanded to take up my words, to surround my affair, and to follow my sunna. Whoever is content with my words has been content with the Qur'an, and whoever mocks my words has mocked the Qur'an." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾.

Eighth: Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: Ibn Mas'ud met a man in the state of ihram wearing his clothes, and he said to him: "Take that off." The man said: "Are you reciting to me a verse from the Book of Allah?" He said: "Yes: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾." Abdullah ibn Muhammad ibn Harun al-Firyabi said: I heard al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, say: "Ask me about whatever you wish, and I will inform you from the Book of Allah and the sunna of your Prophet ﷺ." He said: I asked him, "What do you say, may Allah set you right, about the muhrim who kills a wasp?" He said: "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾."

Sufyan ibn Uyayna narrated to us from Abd al-Malik ibn Umayr, from Ribi ibn Hirash, from Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Follow the two after me, Abu Bakr and Umar." Sufyan ibn Uyayna narrated to us from Mis'ar ibn Kidam, from Qays ibn Muslim, from Tariq ibn Shihab, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he commanded the killing of the wasp.

Our scholars said: this is an answer of the utmost excellence. He issued a legal ruling permitting the killing of a wasp during ihram, and clarified that one follows Umar in this, and that the Prophet ﷺ commanded following him, and that Allah the Exalted commanded accepting what the Prophet ﷺ says. Therefore the permissibility of killing it is derived from the Book and the Sunna. This same meaning has already passed from the statement of Ikrima when he was asked about umm al-walad (slave-mothers), and he said: "They are free," in Surah al-Nisa, at His saying: ﴿Obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you﴾ [al-Nisa: 59] [see vol. 5, pp. 259 and 392].

In Sahih Muslim and elsewhere, from Alqama, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah has cursed the women who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, the women who pluck their facial hair (mutanammisat), the women who file their teeth to appear beautiful (mutafalijat), and those who alter the creation of Allah." [Mutanammisat: those who pluck hair from their faces. Mutafalijat: those who take pains to create gaps between their front teeth and molars.] This reached a woman from the Banu Asad called Umm Ya'qub. She came and said: "I have heard that you cursed such and such!" He said: "Why should I not curse one whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ cursed, and it is in the Book of Allah!" She said: "I have read everything between the two covers and found nothing in it of what you say." He said: "If you had read it, you would have found it! Have you not read: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾?" She said: "Yes." He said: "He has forbidden it..." (the hadith). The matter has already been discussed fully in al-Nisa [see vol. 5, pp. 259 and 392].

Ninth: His saying, ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it﴾. Although it comes with the wording "giving" (itaʼ), which means handing over, its meaning is a command. This is shown by His saying, ﴿and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾, pairing it with the prohibition, and a prohibition is only paired with a command. The proof for understanding this is what we mentioned before, along with the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, peace be upon him: "If I command you to do something, do of it what you are able; and if I forbid you from something, avoid it."

Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning the leaders of the Muslims. They said, regarding the wealth of the polytheists that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had seized: "O Messenger of Allah, take your choice portion (safi) and the quarter, and leave us the rest, for this is how we used to do it in the Jahiliyya." And they recited to him:

"For you is the quarter of it, and the choice portions,
and your judgment, and the nashita, and the fudul."

So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse.

Tenth: His saying, ﴿And fear Allah﴾, that is, the punishment of Allah, for His punishment is severe for whoever disobeys Him. It has also been said: fear Allah regarding His commands and prohibitions, so do not neglect them.

﴿Indeed, Allah is severe in punishment﴾ for whoever opposes what He has commanded him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 59, verse 8:

That is, the fay' (spoils acquired without fighting) and the ghanaʾim (spoils of war) are for the poor Emigrants (al-muhajirun).

It was also said: "so that it does not become a circulating commodity (dulah) among the rich, but rather it belongs to the poor." It was also said: this is an explanation of His words: ﴿and to the near of kin and the orphans and the needy and the wayfarer﴾. When they were mentioned by their categories, it was said: the wealth belongs to these, because they are poor and emigrants, and they have been driven out of their homes, so they are the most deserving of people of it. It was also said: ﴿But Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills﴾ to the poor Emigrants, ﴿so that wealth does not become a circulating commodity among the rich of you﴾ from the sons of this world. It was also said: ﴿and Allah is severe in punishment﴾ toward the Emigrants; that is, He is severe in punishment toward the disbelievers because of the poor Emigrants and on account of them. Among these poor are included those mentioned earlier in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and to the near of kin and the orphans﴾. It was also said: it is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon what preceded, and the conjunction particle (waw) was not used, like your saying: "This wealth is for Zayd, for Bakr, for so-and-so, for so-and-so."

The Emigrants here are those who emigrated to the Prophet ﷺ out of love for him and to support him. Qatadah said: "These are the Emigrants who left behind their homes, their wealth, their families and their homelands out of love for Allah and His Messenger, to the extent that a man among them would tie a stone to his belly to keep his spine upright from hunger, and a man would make a pit in winter, having no covering other than it."

ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abza and Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: "Some of the Emigrants had a slave, a wife, a house and a she-camel on which he would perform Hajj and go out to fight. Allah attributed them to poverty and assigned them a share in the zakat."

The meaning of ﴿who were driven out of their homes﴾ is: the disbelievers of Makkah drove them out, that is, they compelled them to leave. They were one hundred men.

(yabtaghuna) means: they seek.

(fadlan min Allah) means: spoils in this world; (wa-ridwanan) means: in the Hereafter, that is, the pleasure of their Lord.

(wa-yansuruna Allah wa-rasulahu) means: in jihad in the way of Allah.

(ulaika hum al-sadiqun) means: in their action of that. It is narrated that ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, delivered a sermon at al-Jabiyah [a town in Damascus], and said: "Whoever wishes to ask about the Qur'an, let him come to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb; whoever wishes to ask about the inheritance shares (al-faraʾid), let him come to Zayd ibn Thabit; whoever wishes to ask about jurisprudence (al-fiqh), let him come to Muʿadh ibn Jabal; and whoever wishes to ask about wealth, let him come to me, for Allah the Exalted has made me its treasurer and distributor. Indeed, I will begin with the wives of the Prophet ﷺ, giving to them, then the first Emigrants. I and my companions were driven out of Makkah from our homes and our wealth."

There are eleven issues in it.

The first: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who had settled the abode and the faith before them﴾. There is no disagreement that those who settled the abode are the Ansar (the Helpers), who took up residence in Madinah before the Muhajirun (the Emigrants) came to it. The word "al-iman" (the faith) is in the accusative because it is governed by a verb other than "tabawwa'" (settled), since settling (tabawwu') applies to places, and "min qablihim" (before them) is a complement of "tabawwa'." The meaning is: those who settled the abode before the coming of the Muhajirun, and who held the faith and made it sincere, since faith is not a place that one can settle in. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: "So resolve upon your affair, and your partners" (Yunus: 71), meaning: "and call upon your partners." This was mentioned by Abu 'Ali, al-Zamakhshari and others. It falls under the same pattern as the saying: "I fed it straw and cold water." It is also permissible to read it as having an elided genitive, as if He had said: "settled the abode and the places of faith." It is also permissible to read it as governed by what "tabawwa'" implies, as if He had said: "they held fast to the abode and held fast to the faith, and did not part from them." It is also permissible that "tabawwa' al-iman" be a figurative expression, as when one says: "He settled among the Banu so-and-so in their pure lineage." Al-Tabawwu' means establishing oneself and settling. He does not mean that the Ansar believed before the Muhajirun, but rather that they believed before the Prophet's (ﷺ) migration to them.

The second: It has also been disputed whether this verse is detached from what precedes it or joined to it. Some held that it is joined to His saying: "for the poor Emigrants," and that all the verses in Surat al-Hashr are joined one to another. Had they reflected on this fairly, they would have found it contrary to what they claimed, because Allah, Exalted is He, says: "He it is who expelled those who disbelieved among the People of the Book from their homes at the first gathering. You did not think they would go forth..." up to "the defiant ones" (al-Hashr: 2–5), and so He informs about the Banu al-Nadir and the Banu Qaynuqa'. Then He says: "And what Allah bestowed as fay' upon His Messenger from them, you did not press forward against it with horse or camel, but Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills" (al-Hashr: 6). So He informs that this belongs to the Messenger (ﷺ), because no one had pressed forward against it when they were left alone. As for the fighting that had preceded against them and the cutting of their trees, they had already withdrawn from it and that matter had ended. Then He says: "What Allah bestowed as fay' upon His Messenger from the people of the townships belongs to Allah and to the Messenger and to the near kin and the orphans and the needy and the wayfarer" (al-Hashr: 7). This is a statement not joined to the first. Likewise, "and those who had settled the abode and the faith" is the beginning of a statement in praise of the Ansar and in commendation of them, for they yielded that fay' to the Muhajirun. It is as if He had said: "The fay' is for the poor Emigrants, and the Ansar love those who emigrated to them, and do not envy them for what came to them of the fay'." Likewise, "and those who came after them" (al-Hashr: 10) is the beginning of a statement, and its predicate is "they say: Our Lord, forgive us" (al-Hashr: 10). Ismail ibn Ishaq said: His saying "and those who had settled the abode" and "those who came after them" are joined to what precedes, and that they are partners in the fay', meaning: this wealth belongs to the Muhajirun and to those who had settled the abode.
