Malik ibn Aws said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) recited this verse, "The alms are only for the poor" (al-Tawbah: 60), and said: "This is for those." Then he recited, "And know that whatever you gain of anything, a fifth of it belongs to Allah" (al-Anfal: 41), and said: "This is for those." Then he recited, "What Allah bestowed as fay' upon His Messenger..." until He reached "for the poor Emigrants, and those who had settled the abode and the faith, and those who came after them," and then said: "If I live, the shepherd will certainly come, while he is at Sarw Himyar, and his share of it will not have made his brow sweat."

It has been said that he (ʿUmar) gathered the Muhajirun and the Ansar and consulted them about what Allah had opened to him of that. He said to them: "Consider the matter and reflect upon it, then come to me in the morning." He pondered during that night, and it became clear to him that these verses had been revealed concerning that. When they came to him in the morning, he said: "Last night I passed by the verses that are in Surat al-Hashr," and he recited, "What Allah bestowed as fay' upon His Messenger from the people of the townships..." up to His saying, "for the poor Emigrants." When he reached His saying, "Those are the truthful ones" (al-Hujurat: 15), he said: "These are not for these alone." And he recited His saying: "And those who came after them... up to... Compassionate, Merciful" (al-Hashr: 10). Then he said: "No one among the people of Islam remains except that he has entered into this." And Allah knows best.

The third: Malik narrated from Zayd ibn Aslam, from his father, that 'Umar said: "Were it not for those who will come after the people, no township would be conquered except that I would divide it, just as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) divided Khaybar." In the widely transmitted reports from many chains: 'Umar left the fertile lands (sawad) of Iraq and Egypt, and whatever was conquered there of spoils, to be part of the allowances of the fighters and the provisions of the common folk and the dependents. Al-Zubayr, Bilal and more than one of the Companions wanted him to divide what had been conquered among them, but he disliked that from them. Scholars differed about what he did in this matter. It was said: he sought the consent of the army, so whoever was pleased to give up his share without compensation, so that it would remain for the Muslims as a common resource, was granted that, and whoever refused, he gave him the price of his share. Whoever says that he left the land only after seeking the consent of the people has made his action like the action of the Prophet (ﷺ), because he divided Khaybar, and since his purchasing them and leaving those who left willingly is equivalent to dividing them. It was also said: he left it without giving anything to the armies. It was also said: he interpreted in this matter the saying of Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He: "for the poor Emigrants... up to... our Lord, You are indeed Compassionate, Merciful," as has preceded. And Allah knows best. [The phrase "and Allah knows best" is missing from the manuscript S.]

The fourth: The scholars differed concerning the division of immovable property ('aqar). Malik said: the ruler may hold it in trust for the welfare of the Muslims. Abu Hanifa said: the ruler has the choice between dividing it or making it an endowment (waqf) for the welfare of the Muslims. Al-Shafi'i said: the ruler does not have the right to withhold it from them without their consent, but rather must divide it among them like the rest of the wealth. Whoever is willingly content to give up his right, the ruler may make it an endowment for them, and that is permitted for him. Whoever is not content, he has more right to his property. 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) sought the consent of the spoils-takers and bought their shares from them. I say: On this view, His saying, "and those who came after them" (al-Hashr: 10), would be detached from what precedes it, and they are encouraged to supplicate for the earlier ones and to praise them.

The fifth: Ibn Wahb said: I heard Malik mention the excellence of Madinah over other regions, and he said: "Madinah was settled through faith and emigration, while other townships were conquered by the sword." Then he recited, "and those who had settled the abode and the faith before them, they love those who emigrated to them," to the end of the verse. This matter has already been discussed, as has the excellence of prayer in the two mosques, al-Masjid al-Haram and the Mosque of Madinah, so there is no point in repeating it.

The sixth: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they find in their breasts no need for what they have been given﴾. That is, they do not envy the Muhajirun for what they were singled out with from the fay' wealth and other things. So the people have said. In it there is an estimation of two elided genitives, the meaning being: "a trace of need from the loss of what they were given." Anything a person finds in his breast that he needs to remove is a "need" (hajah). The Muhajirun were living in the homes of the Ansar. When the Prophet (ﷺ) acquired the wealth of the Banu al-Nadir, he summoned the Ansar and thanked them for what they had done with the Muhajirun in housing them in their homes and sharing their wealth with them. Then he said: "If you wish, I will divide what Allah has bestowed upon me from the Banu al-Nadir between you and them, and the Muhajirun will remain as they are, dwelling in your homes and with your wealth. And if you wish, I will give it to them, and they will leave your homes." Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said: "Rather, we will divide it among the Muhajirun, and they will remain in our homes as they have been." The Ansar called out: "We are content and we submit, O Messenger of Allah." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Allah, have mercy upon the Ansar and the sons of the Ansar." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave to the Muhajirun and gave nothing to the Ansar except the three whom we have mentioned. [See p. 11 of this part.]

It is possible that He means by "and they find in their breasts no need for what they have been given" that when it is little they are content with it and satisfied with it. They were in this state during the life of the Prophet (ﷺ), in this world, and then they were in it after his death (ﷺ) according to the rule of this world. The Prophet (ﷺ) had warned them and said: "You will see after me a preference for others, so be patient until you meet me at the Basin (al-Hawd)."

The seventh: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they prefer others over themselves, even though poverty was upon them﴾. In the Tirmidhi, from Abu Hurayrah: a man had a guest stay with him, and he had nothing except his own food and the food of his children. He said to his wife: "Put the children to sleep, extinguish the lamp, and bring out for the guest what you have." Then this verse was revealed: "And they prefer others over themselves, even though poverty was upon them." He (al-Tirmidhi) said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith." Muslim also narrated it. It was also narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "I am exhausted." He sent to one of his wives, and she said: "By Him who sent you with the truth, I have nothing but water." Then he sent to another, and she said the same, until all of them said the same: "No, by Him who sent you with the truth, I have nothing but water." He said: "Who will host this man tonight, may Allah have mercy on him?" A man from the Ansar stood up and said: "I, O Messenger of Allah." He took him to his household and said to his wife: "Do you have anything?" She said: "No, except the food of my children." He said: "Distract them with something, and when our guest enters, extinguish the lamp and show him that we are eating. When he reaches out to eat, get up to the lamp until you extinguish it." He said: "They sat down, and the guest ate. When morning came, he went to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has been amazed at what you two did for your guest tonight.'" [The word "amazed" means that this matter was great in His estimation and weighed heavily upon Him; ascribing amazement to Allah is figurative, since nothing about the causes of things is hidden from Him.]

In another report from Abu Hurayrah: A man came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to have him host him, but he did not have anything to offer. He said: "Is there no man who will host this one, may Allah have mercy on him?" A man from the Ansar called Abu Talhah stood up. He took him to his household... and he related the hadith in a manner similar to the previous one, and mentioned in it the revelation of the verse. Al-Mahdawi mentioned from Abu Hurayrah that this was revealed concerning Thabit ibn Qays and a man

From among the Ansar: Thabit stayed with him. He was called Abu al-Mutawakkil. Abu al-Mutawakkil had nothing but food for himself and his children. So he said to his wife, "Put out the lamp and put the children to sleep," and he set what he had before his guest.

Al-Nahhas also mentioned this. He said: Abu Hurayrah said: Thabit ibn Qays was a guest of a man from the Ansar called Abu al-Mutawakkil. He had nothing but food for himself and his children. So he said to his wife, "Put out the lamp and put the children to sleep." Then this was revealed: "They prefer [others] above themselves, even though they themselves are in need," up to His words, "It is those who are the successful."

It was also said that the one who did this was Abu Talhah.

Al-Qushayri, Abu Nasr Abd al-Rahim ibn Abd al-Karim, mentioned: Ibn Umar said: A head of a sheep was given as a gift to a man among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He said, "My brother so-and-so and his dependants are more in need of this than we are." So he sent it to them. Then one sent it to another, until it passed through seven households, and it returned to the first. Then this was revealed: "They prefer [others] above themselves."

Al-Tha'labi related this from Anas: A head of a sheep was given as a gift to a man among the Companions, and he was in hardship. He sent it to a neighbour of his. It passed through seven persons in seven houses, then returned to the first. Then this was revealed: "They prefer [others] above themselves," the verse.

Ibn Abbas said: The Prophet said to the Ansar on the day of Banu al-Nadir: "If you wish, I will divide [the property] of your homes and wealth among the Muhajirun, and you will share with them in this spoil. And if you wish, your homes and your wealth will remain yours, and we will not divide any of the spoil among you." The Ansar said, "Rather, we will divide our homes and our wealth among our brothers, and we will prefer them over ourselves in the spoil." Then this was revealed: "They prefer [others] above themselves," the verse.

The first account is more sound. In the two Sahihs, from Anas: A man used to give the Prophet ﷺ some palm trees from his land, until Qurayzah and al-Nadir were conquered for him. After that, he began returning to them what he had given him. This is the wording of Muslim.

Al-Zuhri related from Anas ibn Malik: When the Muhajirun came to Madinah from Makkah, they arrived with nothing in their hands. The Ansar were the people of the land and the estates. The Ansar shared their produce with them, giving them half the fruit of their wealth each year, while they took care of the work and the expenses. The mother of Anas ibn Malik was called Umm Sulaym, and she was the mother of Abd Allah ibn Abi Talhah, who was a brother of Anas through their mother. Umm Anas had given the Messenger of Allah ﷺ some of her palm trees [[al-adhdhaq, with the ʿayn vowelled with kasra, plural of adhq, which is with fatha; it means palm trees.]]. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave them to Umm Ayman, his freedwoman, and then to Usamah ibn Zayd.

Ibn Shihab said: Anas ibn Malik informed me that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ finished fighting the people of Khaybar and returned to Madinah, the Muhajirun returned to the Ansar the gifts they had been given from their fruit. He said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned my mother's palm trees to her, and he gave Umm Ayman in their place from his own orchard. Muslim also transmitted this.

The Eighth [issue]: Ithar (altruism, preferring others) is putting others before oneself, in one's own worldly portions and in one's desires, while desiring the religious portions. It arises from strength of certainty, firmness of love, and patience with hardship. It is said: "I preferred him with such-and-such," meaning I singled him out with it and favoured him. The object of ithar is omitted, meaning: they prefer them over themselves with their wealth and their dwellings, not from wealth but while they themselves are in need of these things, as has been explained previously.

In the Muwatta' of Malik: It reached him from Aisha, the wife of the Prophet ﷺ, that a poor man asked her while she was fasting, and there was in her house only a loaf of bread. She said to a freedwoman of hers, "Give it to him." The freedwoman said, "Do you not have anything to break your fast with?" She said, "Give it to him." She said: So she did. She said: When evening came, a household, or a person, gave us a gift that was not usually given to us: a sheep, wrapped [[i.e., it was wrapped in loaves; its meaning will come more clearly below. Her words, "that was not usually given to us," mean that Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, did not know of this and did not count on it, so as to rely on it; but Allah, glory be to Him, compensated her from where she did not expect.
(Sharh al-Muwatta').]]. Aisha called me and said, "Eat from this, for it is better than your loaf."

Our scholars said: This is from the profitable wealth, and the pure deed with Allah, the Exalted, He hastens from it what He wills, and that does not diminish what is stored for Him. Whoever leaves something for the sake of Allah does not find its loss. Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, in this deed of hers, is among those whom Allah praised for preferring [others] over themselves while they were in need. Whoever does this has been protected from the greed of his soul and attains a success after which there is no loss.

The meaning of "a sheep and its wrapping": the Arabs, or some of the Arabs, or some of their classes, used to make this from their food. They would take a sheep or a lamb after skinning it, cover it entirely with wheat dough, wrap it in it, then hang it in the oven. Nothing of its fat would escape except into that wrapping, and this was among the finest food to them.

Al-Nasa'i related from Nafi': Ibn Umar fell ill and craved grapes. A cluster was bought for him for a dirham. A poor man came and asked, and he said, "Give it to him." Someone went against him and bought it for a dirham, then brought it to Ibn Umar. The poor man came and asked again, and he said, "Give it to him." Then someone went against him again and bought it for a dirham, then brought it to him. The beggar wanted to return, but he was prevented. Had Ibn Umar known that it was that same cluster, he would not have tasted it, because what has been given for the sake of Allah does not return to him.

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned, saying: Muhammad ibn Mutarrif informed us, saying: Abu Hazim narrated to us, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Sa'id ibn Yarbu', from Malik al-Dar: Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, took four hundred dinars and put them in a purse. Then he said to the boy, "Go with them to Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, then linger in the house a while so that you see what he does with them." The boy went with them to him and said, "The Commander of the Believers says to you: put this towards some of your needs." He said, "May Allah connect him and have mercy on him." Then he said, "Come here, girl. Take these seven [dinars] to so-and-so, and these five to so-and-so," until he sent them all out. The boy returned to Umar and informed him. He found that he had prepared the same amount for Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and he said, "Go with this to Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and linger in the house a while until you see what he does." The boy went with it to him and said, "The Commander of the Believers says to you: put this towards some of your needs." He said, "May Allah have mercy on him and connect him." He said, "Girl, go to the house of so-and-so with such-and-such, and to the house of so-and-so with such-and-such." Then Mu'adh's wife looked out and said, "And us! By Allah, we are needy, so give us some." Only two dinars remained in the purse, which he had brought to her. The boy returned to Umar and informed him, and Umar was pleased with this and said, "They are brothers, some of them from others!"

A similar account is related from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, regarding Mu'awiyah giving her [money]. It was ten thousand, and al-Munkadir had entered upon her [[there is a blank after the word "upon her" in the manuscripts ḥ, z, s, h; the copyist noted this by saying: a blank in the original.]].

If it is said: Authentic reports have come forbidding giving away all that a person owns. It is answered: That was only disliked for one who cannot be trusted to be patient with poverty, and who fears he will be exposed to begging once he has lost what he spends. As for the Ansar, whom Allah praised for preferring [others] over themselves, they were not of this description. Rather, they were as Allah, the Exalted, said: "those who are patient in misfortune and adversity and in time of battle" [al-Baqarah: 177] [[see vol. 2, p. 243.]]. Preferring [others] was better for them than withholding. For one who cannot be patient and who would expose himself to begging, withholding is better than preferring [others].

It is related that a man came to the Prophet ﷺ with something like an egg of gold and said, "This is a charity." He threw it at him and said: "One of you comes with all that he owns, gives it in charity, then sits asking people for alms." And Allah knows best.

The Ninth [issue]: Ithar with oneself is above ithar with wealth, even if it returns to the self. Among the well-known proverbs is:

"Giving one's soul is the utmost limit of generosity" [[This is from a verse by Muslim ibn al-Walid, whose first half is:
"You give your soul when you are the one who withholds it."
He means: you give your soul in battle, when you are the one who withholds it from dishonour. It is also reported as:
"He gives his soul when the generous one withholds it."]]

Among the elegant expressions of the Sufis in defining love is that it is ithar. Do you not see that the wife of the Aziz, when her love for Yusuf, peace be upon him, reached its height, she preferred him over herself and said: "It was I who sought to seduce him" [Yusuf: 51]. The best of giving one's soul is giving it for the protection of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. In the Sahih, Abu Talhah shielded the Prophet ﷺ with his body on the day of Uhud, and the Prophet ﷺ would look out to see the people. Abu Talhah would say to him, "Do not raise yourself, O Messenger of Allah! They will not hit you! My neck is in front of your neck." He protected the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with his hand, and it was paralysed.

Hudhayfah al-Adawi said: I set out on the day of al-Yarmuk seeking my cousin, and with me was some water. I was saying, "If he has some breath left, I will give him water." Then I found him, and I said, "Shall I give you water?" He nodded his head, yes. Then I heard a man saying, "Ah! Ah!" My cousin signalled to me to go to him. It was Hisham ibn al-As. I said, "Shall I give you water?" He signalled yes. Then he heard another saying, "Ah! Ah!" Hisham signalled to me to go to him. I went to him, and he had died. I returned to Hisham, and he had died. I returned to my cousin, and he had died.

Abu Yazid al-Bistami said: No one overcame me as a young man of the people of Balkh overcame me. He came to us on pilgrimage and said to me, "O Abu Yazid, what is the limit of asceticism according to you?" I said, "If we find, we eat, and if we lack, we are patient." He said, "This is how the dogs of Balkh are with us." I said, "And what is the limit of asceticism according to you?" He said, "If we lack, we give thanks, and if we find, we prefer [others]."

Dhu al-Nun al-Misri was asked: What is the limit of the ascetic whose breast is expanded? He said three things: dispersing what is gathered, abandoning the pursuit of what is lost, and ithar at the time of sustenance.

It is related from Abu al-Hasan al-Antaki that more than thirty men gathered with him in a village of the villages of al-Rayy, and with them were a counted number of loaves that would not satisfy them all. They broke the loaves, put out the lamp, and sat down for the meal. When it was removed, the food was still intact, and no one had eaten any of it, out of preferring his companion over himself.

The Tenth [issue]: His words, exalted is He [[the phrase "his words, exalted is He" is missing from manuscript s.]]: "and even though they themselves are in need." Khasasah is the need by which one's condition is disturbed. Its root is from ikhtisas, which is being alone with a matter. So khasasah is being alone with need, meaning: even though they had poverty and need. From this is the poet's saying:
"As for spring, when there is khasasah,
the sick one lives by it, and the poor one grows rich."

The Eleventh [issue]: His words, exalted is He: "And whoever is protected from the greed of his own soul, it is those who are the successful" [al-Hashr: 9]. Shuhh and bukhl (stinginess) are the same. It is said: "a man who is shahih," between shuhh, shahh, and shahhakah. Amr ibn Kulthum said:
"You see the stingy, tight-fisted one, when the cup is passed around,
disgraced regarding his wealth in it."
[[In al-Tabrizi's commentary: "al-lahiz: the narrow, stingy one. It is said: he is the bad-tempered, base one. His words, 'when it is passed around him,' means: when wine circulates much around him, he humiliates his wealth. It is said: 'a disgracer of his wealth' when he is generous, and 'a holder of his wealth dear' when he is stingy."]]

Some lexicographers considered *shuhh* (greed-driven miserliness) to be worse than *bukhl* (miserliness). In al-Sihah (the dictionary of al-Jawhari), *shuhh* is "*bukhl* together with greed." One says *shahha* (in the *kasra* form, *shahiht*) *yashuhhu*, and also *shahhat* *tashuhhu* and *tashihhu*. A man is *shahih*, and people are *shihad* and *ashihhah*.

The meaning of the verse is: *shuhh* regarding zakat and what is not obligatory, such as keeping ties with relatives, hospitality, and similar things. Whoever spends in these matters is not stingy or miserly, even if he withholds from himself. Whoever spends lavishly on himself and does not give in the zakat and good deeds we have mentioned has not been protected from the *shuhh* of his own soul.

Al-Aswad narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that a man came to him and said: "I fear that I may have perished." He asked: "What is that?" The man said: "I heard Allah, Mighty and Majestic, say: ﴿And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul, it is those who are the successful﴾ [59:9], and I am a stingy man who can hardly bring anything out of his hand." Ibn Mas'ud said: "That is not the *shuhh* that Allah, Exalted, mentioned in the Qur'an. The *shuhh* that Allah, Exalted, mentioned in the Qur'an is that you consume the wealth of your brother unjustly. What you have is *bukhl*, and *bukhl* is a wretched thing." Thus, may Allah be pleased with him, he distinguished between *shuhh* and *bukhl*.

Tawus said: "*Bukhl* is when a person withholds what is in his hand, and *shuhh* is when he is greedy for what is in the hands of people. He wants what is in their hands, whether lawful or unlawful, and is never content."

Ibn Jubayr said: "*Shuhh* is withholding zakat and hoarding what is unlawful."

Ibn 'Uyayna said: "*Shuhh* is injustice."

Al-Layth said: "*Shuhh* is abandoning the obligations and violating the prohibitions."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Whoever follows his desire and does not accept faith, that is the stingy person."

Ibn Zayd said: "Whoever does not take anything that Allah has forbidden him, and whose *shuhh* does not prevent him from giving anything that Allah has commanded him to give, Allah has protected him from the *shuhh* of his soul."

Anas said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever pays zakat, hosts the guest, and gives in times of calamity, is free of *shuhh*."

From Anas also: the Prophet (ﷺ) used to supplicate: "O Allah, I seek refuge in You from the *shuhh* of my soul, its extravagance, and its whisperings."

Abu al-Hayyaj al-Asadi said: "I saw a man in the circumambulation praying: 'O Allah, protect me from the *shuhh* of my soul,' and he added nothing to it. So I said to him, and he said: 'When I am protected from the *shuhh* of my soul, I will not steal, I will not commit adultery, and I will not do such things.'" The man was 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf.

I say: This is indicated by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Beware of injustice, for injustice will be darkness on the Day of Resurrection. Beware of *shuhh*, for *shuhh* destroyed those before you; it led them to shed their blood and to make lawful what was forbidden to them." I have explained this at the end of Surah Al 'Imran [See vol. 4, p. 293.]

Kisra said to his companions: "What is most harmful to the son of Adam?" They said: "Poverty." Kisra said: "*Shuhh* is more harmful than poverty, because the poor person, when he finds something, is satisfied, but the stingy person, when he finds something, is never satisfied."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 59, verse 10:

There are four issues in this verse. The first: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who came after them﴾, meaning the Successors (al-tabi'un, the generation after the Companions) and whoever entered Islam until the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Abi Layla said: "People are of three ranks: the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun), those who settled in the abode and the faith (al-Ansar), and those who came after them. So strive not to leave these ranks." Some of them said: "Be a sun; if you cannot, then be a moon; if you cannot, then be a bright star; if you cannot, then be a small star, but from the direction of the light you will not be cut off." The meaning of this is: be an Emigrant. If you say, "I cannot find it," then be an Ansari. If you cannot find that, then act as they acted; if you cannot do that, then love them and seek forgiveness for them as Allah has commanded you. Musab ibn Sa'd narrated: "People are in three ranks. Two ranks have passed, and one rank remains. The best that you can be is to be in this remaining rank." And from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them, that a man came to him and said: "O son of the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), what do you say about Uthman?" He said to him: "O my brother, you are from a people about whom Allah said: ﴿For the poor Emigrants﴾ [59:8], the verse..." He said: "No!" He said: "By Allah, if you are not among the people of that verse [[What is between the brackets is omitted from S and H.]], then you are from a people about whom Allah said: ﴿And those who settled in the abode and the faith﴾ [59:9], the verse..." He said: "No." He said: "By Allah, if you are not among the people of the third verse, you will certainly leave Islam, and it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who came after them say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith﴾ [59:10], the verse."

It has also been said that Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them, narrated from his father that a group of people from Iraq came to him, and they reviled Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, then Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, and they said a great deal. He said to them: "Are you of the first Emigrants?" They said: "No." He said: "Are you of those who settled in the abode and the faith before them?" They said: "No." He said: "You have disassociated yourselves from these two groups! I bear witness that you are not among those about whom Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And those who came after them say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and do not place in our hearts any rancor toward those who believe. Our Lord, You are Kind and Merciful﴾ [59:10]. Rise up; may Allah do to you and do..." This was recorded by al-Nahhas.

The second: This verse is evidence for the obligation of loving the Companions, because He made a share in the fay' (spoils taken without battle) for those who came after them, as long as they maintain their love for them, their allegiance to them, and their seeking forgiveness for them. And whoever reviles them, or reviles one of them, or holds evil beliefs about one of them, has no right to the fay'. This was related from Malik and others. Malik said: "Whoever harbors hatred toward any of the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), or has rancor against them in his heart, has no right in the wealth of the Muslims." Then he recited: ﴿And those who came after them﴾, the verse.

The third: This verse indicates that the most correct of the scholars' opinions is the division of movable property, while leaving land and real estate as a common endowment shared among all Muslims, as Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, did. However, the ruler may exercise independent judgment and implement a decision, so that his action is carried out, because people disagree about it. This verse supports that, because Allah, the Exalted, informed us about the fay' and made it for three groups: the Emigrants and the Ansar, who are known, and ﴿And those who came after them say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith﴾. It is therefore general to all the Successors and those who come after them until the Day of Judgment. In the authentic hadith: The Prophet (ﷺ) went out to the graveyard and said: "Peace be upon you, abode of a believing people, and we, if Allah wills, will join you. I wished that I could see our brothers." They said: "O Messenger of Allah, are we not your brothers?" He said: "Rather, you are my Companions, and our brothers are those who have not yet come." And: "I am your forerunner at the Basin." Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) made clear that their brothers are everyone who comes after them, not as al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said, that they are those who emigrated after that. And from al-Hasan also: ﴿And those who came after them﴾ refers to whoever came to the Prophet (ﷺ) at Medina after the cessation of the Hijrah.

The fourth: His saying, the Exalted: ﴿say﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: saying.

(Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith.) In this there are two views. One: they were commanded to seek forgiveness for those among the believers of the People of the Book who preceded this Ummah. Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "They were commanded to seek forgiveness for them, but they reviled them." The second: they were commanded to seek forgiveness for the earliest foremost ones among the Emigrants and the Ansar. Ibn Abbas said: "Allah, the Exalted, commanded seeking forgiveness for the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ), while He knew that they would be tested." Aisha also said: "You were commanded to seek forgiveness for the Companions of Muhammad, but you reviled them. I heard your Prophet (ﷺ) say: 'This Ummah will not pass away until its last ones curse its first ones.'" Ibn Umar said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'When you see those who revile my Companions, say: May Allah curse the worst of you.'" Al-Awwam ibn Hawshab said: "I met the early part of this Ummah saying: Mention the good qualities of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that hearts are brought together upon them, and do not mention what passed between them, lest you embolden people against them." Al-Sha'bi said: "The Jews and Christians surpassed the Rafidah (Rafidites) in one trait. The Jews were asked: 'Who is the best of your religion's people?' They said: 'The companions of Moses.' The Christians were asked: 'Who is the best of your religion's people?' They said: 'The companions of Jesus.' The Rafidah were asked: 'Who is the worst of your religion's people?' They said: 'The companions of Muhammad. They were commanded to seek forgiveness for them, but they reviled them.' So the sword is drawn against them until the Day of Resurrection; no banner rises for them, no foot is firm for them, and no word unites them. Whenever they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it by spilling their blood and refuting their argument. May Allah protect us and you from misguiding desires."

﴿And do not place in our hearts any rancor toward those who believe﴾, i.e., hatred and envy. ﴿Our Lord, You are Kind and Merciful﴾

The text is a wonder at the Jews' delusion, in regard to what the hypocrites promised them of victory, even though they know that the hypocrites hold to neither a religion nor a scripture. [[In manuscript A: "ʿajab".]] Among the hypocrites were ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, ʿAbd Allah ibn Nabtal, and Rifaʿa ibn Zayd. It is also said: Rafiʿa ibn Tabut and Aws ibn Qayzi. They were from the Ansar (the Helpers of Madina), but they practised hypocrisy, and they said to the Jews of Quraydha and al-Nadir: "If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you." It is also said that this is the statement of the Banu al-Nadir to Quraydha. As for his saying, "and we will never obey anyone against you, ever," they mean Muhammad (ﷺ): "We will not obey him in fighting you." In this there is evidence for the truth of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) from the aspect of knowledge of the unseen, for they were expelled and did not go out, and they were fought and they did not help them, as God, exalted is He, said: "And God bears witness that they are liars" (i.e., in their saying and their deeds).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 59, verse 12:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If they are expelled, they will not go out with them; and if they are fought, they will not help them; and if they help them, they will surely turn their backs; then they will not be helped.﴾ That is, they will be defeated. It has been said: the meaning of "they will not help them" is "willingly." And "if they help them" means "under compulsion," and "they will surely turn their backs." It has also been said: the meaning of "they will not help them" is "they will not persist in helping them." This is on the basis that the two pronouns refer to the same group. It has been said, however, that they refer to different groups, and the meaning is: if the Jews are expelled, the hypocrites will not go out with them; and if they are fought, they will not help them. "And if they help them," that is, if the Jews help the hypocrites, "they will surely turn their backs." It has been said: "If they are expelled, they will not go out with them" means that God knew about them that they would not go out if they were expelled. "And if they are fought, they will not help them" means that God knew this about them. Then He said: "they will surely turn their backs," so He informed of what He had already informed would not happen, how it would happen if it were to happen? This is like His saying: ﴿And if they were returned, they would go back to what they were forbidden﴾ [al-An'am: 28] [see vol. 6, p. 410]. It has also been said: the meaning of "and if they help them" is: if We willed that they help them, We would make that appealing to them, and "they will surely turn their backs."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, you﴾ (O assembly of Muslims) ﴿are greater in fear﴾ (ashaddu rahbah), meaning greater in dread and awe, ﴿in their breasts than Allah.﴾ It refers to the breasts of the Banu al-Nadir. It was also said: it refers to the breasts of the hypocrites. It is possible that it refers to both groups, meaning: they fear you more than they fear their Lord. That is the fear.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not understand﴾, meaning they do not comprehend the extent of Allah's greatness and power.

The Qur'an, the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They will not fight you all together﴾, meaning the Jews, ﴿except in fortified towns﴾, that is, with walls and houses, thinking that these will protect them from you.

﴿Or from behind walls﴾, that is, from behind walls they hide behind out of their cowardice and fear. The reading of the majority is *judurin* (جُدُرٍ) in the plural, which is the preference of Abu 'Ubayda and Abu Hatim, because it corresponds to the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿in fortified towns﴾, and that is plural. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Kathir, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu 'Amr read *jidarin* (جِدَارٍ) in the singular, because the singular conveys the plural. It is narrated from some of the Meccan readers *jadrin* (جَدْرٍ), with a fatha on the *jim* and a sukun on the *dal*, which is a dialect form for *al-jidar* (the wall). It is also possible that its meaning is "from behind their palm trees and their trees." It is said: *ajdara al-nakhlu* (أَجْدَرَ النَّخْلُ), when its shoots appear at the beginning of spring. *Al-judr* is a plant whose singular is *judra*. It is read *judrun* (جُدْرٌ), with a damma on the *jim* and a sukun on the *dal*, as the plural of *al-jidar*. It is also possible that the alif in the singular is like the alif in *kitab*, and in the plural like the alif in *ziraf*. A similar case is *naqatun hijan* and *nuqun hijan*, because you say in the dual *hijanan*; so the word for the singular and the word for the plural became alike in form but different in meaning. This is the statement of Ibn Jinni.

The Qur'an, the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Their might among themselves is severe﴾, meaning the enmity of some of them towards others. Mujahid said: "Their might among themselves is severe" means by words and threats, "we will certainly do such and such." Al-Suddi said: what is meant is the difference of their hearts, so that they do not agree on a single matter. It was said: "Their might among themselves is severe" means that when they do not meet an enemy, they ascribe to themselves strength and might, but when they meet the enemy, they are routed. ﴿You think them united, but their hearts are divided﴾, meaning the Jews and the hypocrites, as Mujahid said. It is also narrated from him that it means the hypocrites. Al-Thawri said: they are the polytheists and the People of the Book. Qatada said: "You think them united" means gathered upon a single matter and opinion, "but their hearts are divided" means scattered. So the people of falsehood have differing opinions, differing testimonies, and differing desires, yet they are united in enmity towards the people of truth. It is also narrated from Mujahid: he meant that the religion of the hypocrites differs from the religion of the Jews, and this was to strengthen the souls of the believers against them. A poet said:

To Allah I complain of an intention that split the staff;
today it is scattered, and yesterday it was closely gathered.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, it is "and their hearts are *ashudd*" (أَشَتُّ), meaning more intensely scattered, that is, more intensely divided.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason﴾, meaning that this scattering and disbelief are because they have no intellect with which they comprehend the command of Allah.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "It refers to Qaynuqa', whom Allah empowered over before Banu al-Nadir." Qatadah said: "It refers to Banu al-Nadir, whom Allah empowered over before Quraydhah." Mujahid said: "It refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh on the day of Badr."

It was also said: "It is general, applying to everyone who was punished for his disbelief before the Banu al-Nadir, from Nuh to Muhammad (ﷺ)."

The meaning of "wabal" (وَبالَ) is the consequence (jaza') of their disbelief. And whoever said they are Banu Quraydhah took "the wabal of their affair" to mean their submission to the judgment of Saʿd ibn Muʿadh, who ruled that their fighting men be killed and their offspring taken captive. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

Whoever said the reference is to Banu al-Nadir said: "The wabal of their affair was the exile and the expulsion." Between al-Nadir and Quraydhah there were two years. The battle of Badr occurred six months before the expedition against Banu al-Nadir, and therefore He said: "qariban" (قَرِيباً, "soon"). Some people have said that the expedition against Banu al-Nadir came after the battle of Uhud.

"And for them is a painful punishment" (﴿وَلَهُمْ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ﴾) in the Hereafter.

"The example of Satan, when he says to man, 'Disbelieve.'" This is a parable (ḍarb mathal) for the hypocrites and the Jews in their forsaking [their allies] and their failure to fulfill their support for them.

The conjunction (ḥarf al-ʿaṭf, the connecting particle) is omitted, and it does not say "wa-kamathali al-shayṭān" (and like the example of Satan), because omitting the conjunction is common, as you say: "You are intelligent, you are generous, you are learned."

It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ):

That the man to whom Satan said "Disbelieve" was a monk, with whom a woman was left who had been afflicted with madness (lamam), so that he might pray for her. Satan adorned [the act] for him, so he had intercourse with her and she became pregnant. Then he killed her out of fear of being exposed. Satan then showed her people where she was, so they came and brought the monk down in order to kill him. Satan came to him and promised that if he prostrated to him, he would save him from them. So he prostrated to him, and [Satan] disowned him and abandoned him.

This was mentioned by al-Qadi Isma'il and ʿAli ibn al-Madini, from Sufyan ibn ʿUyayna, from ʿAmr ibn Dinar, from ʿUrwa ibn ʿAmir, from ʿUbayd ibn Rifa'a al-Zuraqi, from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn ʿAbbas and Wahb ibn Munabbih related its account at length, and their wording differs.

Ibn ʿAbbas said, regarding the words of the Most High, "like the example of Satan":

There was a monk during the interval (al-fatra, the period between prophets) called Barsisa, who had devoted himself to worship in his hermitage for seventy years, never disobeying Allah for the blink of an eye, until he wearied Iblis. So Iblis gathered the rebellious devils and said: "Will none of you take on for me the matter of Barsisa?"

The one called al-Abyad, who was the companion of the prophets (and he is the one who approached the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of Jibril in order to whisper to him in the manner of revelation), said: [And] Jibril came and entered between them, then pushed him with his hand until he fell at the farthest end of India. That is the meaning of the Most High's words: "Possessed of power, with the Lord of the Throne, secure" (al-Takwir 81:20). Then [al-Abyad] said: "I will suffice you for him." So he set out, dressed in the garb of monks, shaved the middle of his head, and came to the hermitage of Barsisa and called out to him, but he did not answer him. Now [Barsisa] would not turn from his prayer except once every ten days, and would not break his fast except once every ten days, and he would sometimes fast for twenty days or more continuously. When al-Abyad saw that [Barsisa] did not answer him, he turned to worship at the base of his hermitage. When Barsisa turned from his prayer, he saw al-Abyad standing and praying in a fine manner of the monks, and he regretted not having answered him. So he said: "What is your need?" [Al-Abyad] said: "That I be with you, that I may learn your discipline, take from your works, and that we may unite in worship." He said: "I am occupied away from you." Then he turned to his prayer, and al-Abyad also turned to prayer. When Barsisa saw the intensity of his diligence and worship, he said to him: "What is your need?" [Al-Abyad] said: "That you permit me to come up to you." So [Barsisa] permitted him, and al-Abyad remained with him for a year, breaking his fast only one day in every forty days, and not turning from his prayer except once every forty days; and at times he extended it to eighty. When Barsisa saw his diligence, his own soul came to regard itself as lacking.

Then al-Abyad said: "I have supplications by which Allah heals the sick, the afflicted, and the insane," and he taught them to him.

Then he came to Iblis and said: "By Allah, I have ruined the man." Then he confronted a man and strangled him, and then said to his family—having appeared in the form of human beings—: "Your companion has madness. Shall I treat him?" They said: "Yes." He said: "I cannot prevail over his jinn, but take him to Barsisa, for with him is the Greatest Name of Allah, which if one asks by it, He gives, and if one calls upon Him by it, He answers." They came to him, and he invoked those supplications, and the devil departed from him.

Then al-Abyad began doing this with people, directing them to Barsisa, and they were cured.

Then he went to a girl, one of the daughters of kings, between three brothers, whose father had been a king; he died and appointed his brother [as successor]. Her paternal uncle was king over the Children of Israel, and he tormented her and strangled her.

Then [al-Abyad] came to them in the form of a physician to treat her and said: "Her devil is a rebellious jinn that cannot be overcome, but take her to Barsisa and leave her with him; when her devil comes, he will supplicate for her and she will be healed." They said: "He will not agree to this for us." He said: "Then build a hermitage beside his hermitage and place her in it, and say: 'She is a trust with you, so seek reward through her.'" They asked him this and he refused, so they built a hermitage and placed the girl in it. When [Barsisa] turned from his prayer, he saw the girl and her beauty, and he was struck with bewilderment. Then the devil came to her and strangled her; he turned from his prayer, supplicated for her, and the devil departed from her. Then he returned to his prayer, and the devil came to her and strangled her again.

He would uncover her and expose her to Barsisa. Then the devil came to him and said: "Woe to you! Have intercourse with her; you will not find the like of her, and you can repent afterward." He did not cease to urge him until he had intercourse with her, and she became pregnant and her pregnancy became apparent.

The devil said to him: "Woe to you! You have been exposed. Will you kill her and then repent, so that you will not be disgraced? If they come to you and ask you, say: 'Her devil came to her and took her away.'" So Barsisa killed her and buried her at night, but Satan took hold of the edge of her garment until it remained protruding from the dust, and Barsisa returned to his prayer.

Then Satan came in a dream to her brothers and said: "Barsisa did such-and-such to your sister; he killed her and buried her in such-and-such a mountain." They were appalled at this and said to Barsisa: "What became of our sister?" He said: "Her devil took her away." They believed him and departed.

Then Satan came to them again in a dream and said: "She is buried in such-and-such a place, and the edge of her garment is protruding from the dust." They went and found her, and they demolished his hermitage, brought him down, strangled him, and carried him to the king, and he confessed against himself, so [the king] ordered his execution.

When he was crucified, Satan said: "Do you know me?" He said: "No, by Allah." He said: "I am your companion who taught you the supplications. Did you not fear Allah? Were you not ashamed, though you are the most devout of the Children of Israel? Then your deed did not suffice you until you disgraced yourself, confessed against yourself, and exposed your likes among people. If you die in this state, none of your peers after you will prosper."

He said: "What shall I do?" He said: "Obey me in one matter, and I will save you from them and take their eyes away from you." He said: "And what is that?" He said: "You prostrate to me one prostration." He said: "I will do it," and he prostrated to him apart from Allah.

Then [Satan] said: "O Barsisa, this is what I wanted from you. The end of your affair is that you disbelieved in your Lord. Indeed, I am free of you; I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds."

Wahb ibn Munabbih said:

There was a worshipper among the Children of Israel, one of the most devout people of his time. In his time there were three brothers who had a sister, who was a virgin, and they had no other sister. A military expedition came out [and went] against all three of them, and they did not know with whom to leave their sister, nor whom to trust with her, nor where to place her.

He said: Their opinion united upon leaving her with the worshipper of the Children of Israel, who was trusted in their own estimation. So they came to him and asked him to keep her, so that she would be in his care and protection until they returned from their campaign. He refused and sought refuge in Allah from them and from their sister.

He said: They did not cease with him until they persuaded him [or: until he obeyed them]. He said: "Lodge her in a house opposite my hermitage." So they lodged her in that house, then departed and left her. She remained in the protection of that worshipper for a time; he would lower food to her from his hermitage, place it at the door of the hermitage, then lock his door and ascend to his hermitage, and then he would command her, and she would come out of her house and take the food that had been placed for her.

He said: Satan dealt subtly with him, and continually encouraged him toward good, and magnified to him the girl's coming out of her house by day, and frightened him that someone might see her and fall in love with her.

He said: He remained in this state for a time. Then Iblis came to him, encouraged him toward good and reward, and said to him: "If you were to walk to her with her food until you placed it in her house, it would be greater for your reward." He said: He did not cease with him until he walked to her with her food and placed it in her house.

He said: He remained in that for a time. Then Iblis came to him, encouraged him toward good and urged him to it, and said: "If you were to speak with her and converse with her, so that she would be at ease with your talk, for she has become extremely lonely." He said: He did not cease with him until he talked with her for a time, looking down upon her from the top of his hermitage.

He said: Then after that Iblis came to him and said: "If you were to come down to her, sit at the door of your hermitage, and converse with her, while she sits at the door of her house and converses with you, it would be more companionable for her." He did not cease with him until he brought him down and seated him at the door of his hermitage, conversing with her, while the girl came out of her house, and they remained for a time talking together. Then Iblis came to him, encouraged him toward good and reward in what he did with her, and said: "If you went out of the door of your hermitage and sat near the door of her house, it would be more companionable for her." He did not cease with him until he did this.

He said: They remained for a time. Then Iblis came to him, encouraged him toward good and toward the goodly reward for what he did with her, and said to him: "If you drew close to the door of her house, talked with her, and she did not come out of her house..." So he did it.

He said: He would come down from his hermitage and sit at the door of her house and talk with her.

They remained in this for a while. Then Iblis came to him and said: "If you entered the house with her, talking with her, and did not leave her to show her face to anyone, it would be better for you." He did not cease with him until he entered the house, and he would talk with her all day; when evening came, he would ascend to his hermitage.

He said: Then Iblis came to him after that, and he did not cease adorning her for him until the worshipper struck her thigh and kissed her.

Iblis did not cease with him, making her beautiful in his eyes and enticing him, until he had intercourse with her and made her pregnant. She bore him a boy. Iblis came to him and said: "What do you think, if the brothers of this girl come and she has borne a child from you? What will you do? I am not sure you will not be exposed, or that they will not expose you! So go to her son, slaughter him, and bury him, for she will keep silent about you out of fear of her brothers, lest they discover what you did to her." He did so.

[Iblis] said to him: "Do you think she will conceal from her brothers what you did to her and that you killed her son? Take her, slaughter her, and bury her with her son."

He did not cease with him until he slaughtered her and cast her into the pit with her son, closed over them a great rock, leveled the earth over them, and ascended to his hermitage to worship there. He remained thus as long as Allah willed, until her brothers returned from the military campaign. They came to him and asked him about her. He announced her death to them, showed compassion for her, wept for them, and said: "She was the best of servants; this is her grave, so look at it."

Her brothers came to the grave, wept over her grave, showed compassion for her, and stayed at her grave for some days, then they departed to their families.

When night fell upon them and they took their beds, Satan came to them in the form of a traveling man. He began with the eldest of them and asked him about their sister. He told him what the worshipper had said, of her death and his compassion for her, and how he had shown them the place of her grave. Satan denied this and said: "He has not told you the truth about your sister's affair. He has made your sister pregnant and she bore a son from him; he slaughtered him and slaughtered her with him, out of fear of you, and cast her into a pit he dug behind the door of the house where she was, on the right of whoever enters it."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 59, verse 16–17 (part 2 of 2):

"So set out and enter the house where she was, on the right of whoever enters it. For you will find them both there together, just as I have told you."
He said:
And he came to the middle one in his sleep and said to him the same thing.
Then he came to the youngest of them and said to him the same thing.
When the people awoke, they awoke astonished at what each of them had seen.
Some of them turned to others, each one saying:
"We have seen a marvel," and each told the others what he had seen.
The eldest of them said:
"This is a dream that is nothing, so let us go on and leave this alone."
The youngest of them said:
"I will not go on until I come to that place and look into it."
He said:
So they all set out until they entered the house where their sister was. They opened the door and searched the place that had been described to them in their dream, and they found their sister and her son slaughtered in the pit, just as they had been told. They asked the worshipper, and he confirmed the words of Iblis regarding what he had done to them both.
[[That is, they sought help from him against him, and he gave them justice against him.]] So their king sought redress against him, and he was brought down from his hermitage. They brought him forward to be crucified, and when they had set him upon the wood, Satan came to him and said:
"You know that I am your companion who tempted you regarding the woman, until you made her pregnant and slaughtered her and slaughtered her son. If you obey me today and disbelieve in God who created you, I will free you from what you are in."
He said:
So the worshipper disbelieved in God, and when he disbelieved, Satan left him between himself and his companions, and they crucified him.
He said:
Concerning him this verse was revealed: "Like the example of Satan when he says to man, 'Disbelieve.' But when he disbelieves, he says, 'Indeed, I am free of you; indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.'" ... to the words "...the recompense of the wrongdoers."
Ibn Abbas said: God struck this as an example for the hypocrites with the Jews. That is because God Most High commanded His Prophet, peace be upon him, to expel Banu al-Nadir from Madinah. The hypocrites secretly sent word to them: "Do not leave your homes; if they fight you, we will be with you, and if they expel you, we will be with you." So they fought the Prophet (ﷺ), and the hypocrites abandoned them and disowned them, just as Satan disowned Barsisa the worshipper. After that, the monks would only walk about with caution [[That is, they would show reconciliation and agreement while inwardly being otherwise.]] and concealment. The people of depravity and wickedness became bold toward the rabbis and accused them with slander and ugliness, until the case of Umm Jurayj the monk, whom God cleared. After that the monks were relieved and appeared openly to the people. It was also said: the meaning is that the example of the hypocrites in their treachery toward Banu al-Nadir is like the example of Iblis when he said to the disbelievers of Quraysh: "No one among the people can overcome you today, and indeed I am your protector" [al-Anfal: 48], the verse. Mujahid said: the word "man" here means all people, in the deception of Satan toward them. The meaning of His words, "when he says to man, 'Disbelieve'," is that he led him astray until he said, "Indeed, I am disbelieving." Satan's words, "Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds," are not literal; they are only a way of disowning the man, and so they confirm His words, "Indeed, I am free of you." Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read the yā' in "innī" with a fatha, while the rest read it with a sukun.
("So the end of both of them was") meaning: the end of Satan and that man ("that they are both in the Fire, abiding therein"). It is accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). The dual is clear for those who take the verse as specific to the monk and Satan. For those who take it in the sense of the category, the meaning is: "the end of the two groups or two kinds was..." The word "'aqibatahuma" is accusative as the predicate of "kana," and the subject is "annahuma fi al-nar." Al-Hasan read "fa-kana 'aqibatuhuma" with a raf' (nominative), the opposite of that. Al-A'mash read "khalidani fiha" with a raf', which contradicts the written form. He made it nominative as the predicate of "anna," and the adverbial phrase is cancelled.

"The example of Satan, when he says to man, 'Disbelieve.'" This is a parable (ḍarb mathal) for the hypocrites and the Jews in their forsaking [their allies] and their failure to fulfill their support for them.
